review_headline: A must see for Strand fans and anyone interested in photographic history.
review_body:
This is a well researched and informative documentary, and worth watching just for the interviews with Georgia O'Keefe. How they got her to agree to be interviewed, I don't know, but it says something about the producers that they were able to accomplish this.

We've all seen Mr. Strand's photos, so I think the whole point in watching a movie about him is to learn more about him and his life.
I have to disagree with the reviewer who thought the (quite brief, actually) segment about his career in film making was slow, as my impression was quite the opposite, and since this is a documentary film and Mr. Strand spent many years as a movie cameraman it's completely logical that this would also be a part of the film, not just his still photography. I thought this segment was very interesting, especially to see his film making style, which reminded me of Sergei Eisenstein's, and which we probably won't see anywhere else, and to learn that he was taking on very serious subjects such as racial intolerance, the KKK, and McCarthyism. Also that his decision to move to Europe was largely because of these issues.

Seeing Mr. Strand wielding his monstrously huge Graflex SLR (5x7?) was also a highlight.

The musical soundtrack was nothing special, kind of typical of a low budget documentary, but I wasn't watching the movie to listen to the music. The "Ken Burns" style of showing the photos was the weakest and most distracting part of the film for me. I felt that the film makers should have displayed the photos in full view first, and then panned around if they felt the need to push that button on iMovie. If the rest of the film had not been so informative I would have knocked a star off for this, but there was so much else about it that was really good that I kept it at five.

I was not surprised at the end to learn from the credits that this film was funded by the Canadian National Film Board. I have watched numerous documentaries funded by this agency, and they have all been of high quality. One can also go to their website and watch a lot of movies for free. Most of them were made by the CBC.

review_headline: known as the Reich's best tactical defensive commander
review_body: Spectacular portrayal of the United States Army and their charlie foxtrot WW II "campaign" on the Siegfied Line in the Hurtgen Forest in late 1944. Referred to as the "Forest in Hell" the U.S. Army brass sacrificed the lives of approximately 33,000 troops, many having just arrived in France and sent to the front with no combat experience. For four months from September to December 1944 approximately ten infantry division's of General Omar Bradley's VII Corps, First Army engaged in a series of fierce and viscous battles against thirteen infantry divisions of Field Marshall Walter Model, known as the Reich's best tactical defensive commander. The losses on both sides was staggering with nothing gained by either. Top flight talent went into the production of this miniseries.  The battlefield scenes reminded me of the realism and gore of the the movie "Saving Private Ryan" directed by the same Spielberg/Hanks duo. Those scenes are hard to watch, but accurately convey the chaos and intensity as well as the random impact of violence on soldiers and marines in battle.  it's good to be reminded of the island-based Pacific campaign which is sometimes overlooked in favor of the land-based European theater in WWII.  This is basically a Marine story.  Among the crowd a few individuals are singled out to personalize the impact of war on families.  By the end of the miniseries these individuals come into sharp focus whereas they tend to get lost in the crowd in the first few episodes.  There are simply too many faces to sort through.  Credits at the end of the miniseries show a few of the actual men and women whose experiences provide the basis for the stories that are told.  Unfortunately issues of race in WWII are entirely ignored in this miniseries - which pretty much reflects how the military (and the nation) functioned at the time.

Great show and wish there were other great programs like this one! The Era of this show starts off Pre-WW1 and takes you down the years to come. The show features this era's Aristocrats, their employees, and the village. Throughout the show you get a take on the different classes of society and that each has their own challenges/problems. With these obstacles and the division of classes, the show proves that people are/can be compassionate no matter where they are in society. The servants take pride in their work and care greatly for their employers. The employers in turn also care greatly for their servants, often stepping in to lend a helping hand if one becomes ill or is in a bad situation. It is displayed in a more compassionate way, unlike you would imagine. Of course they are servants and you see the services they provide for their employers, not saying it is all roses, but is written very well. Overall I think this show is brilliantly done! It is elegant, features great scenery, great actors, and love the touch of the subtle witty humor. Violet Crawley (Countess of Grantham) is brilliantly played for many reasons, I fell in love with her touch of humor,
one-liners, and her mysterious ways. Deep down Old Grandma does show compassion on her terms!

First of all, we have a Roku plus an Amazon Prime account and this film was part of my free Prime streaming. Many free things have been showing up in odd queues on menus I usually don't peruse. Very odd. Anyway, onto the film...

I, too, was mesmerized by this film despite its very measured pace and unusual story line. I love both Maggie Smith and Ruth Wilson and I was able to believe in Ruth as a young Maggie. I very much liked the young man at the mansion...he was the modern character, in contrast to Maggie's current - and Ruth's performance as the younger self - and while he was young and contemporary, he was empathetic, caring and sensitive to the older woman's need to express her story and be cared for when the memories overtook her. I liked that.

I will say that David Walliams was downright creepy as Greville White. He gave me chills right from the beginning, with his big face and quiet, conspiratorial whisperings to guests, who paled and inwardly seemed to shrivel after he passed. The suspense of Mary (Ruth) wanting to meet him was terrific. You knew it was going to happen and when it did, it was as odd and faintly dangerous as I knew it would be. It was truly difficult to know how to take him...and that was the point, right?

People seem confused by the plot. I see it as the story of an intelligent, modern-thinking young woman who is emotionally abused by this man. What he told Mary in the wine cellar is unforgivable. I see him as a psychopath, really. He took perverse delight in telling her horrid, repulsive, even criminal things about people she knows...and sickly delights in ruining her life as she hold the knowledge and images within, unable to ever forget - or move on with her career. In her old age, revisiting the mansion where it all happened, we see that she is still haunted and scarred. So sad.

The fact that Greville never ages does make for some ambiguity, which only enhances the spooky feel to the film. Personally, I loved it and recommend it to anyone who loves good British movies and slightly spooky, unusual stories.to the film. review_headline: Glory is by far the best but not the most accurate Civil War epic drama
review_body: Glory is by far the best but NOT the most accurate Civil War epic drama. Due to the potential to tell the heroic actions of the first Federal volunteer all Black regiment in the Civil War it comes up short, very short. I am happy both Morgan Freeman and Denzel Washington help carry the story, but the truth is the 54th was NOT made up of former and run-away slaves. It was made up of very highly educated and mostly college educated "FREEDMEN". They were (accurately portrayed very religious) but there were many missed opportunities to tell the true history. Frederick Douglass' eldest son was the 1st Sergeant Major, not a former wise old grave digger. Color seargent William Carney was the 1st Black soldier the be awarded the MOH. He didn't die in Battery Wagner. He was multiple wounded. Col. Robert G. Shaw was accurately portrayed by Matthew Broderick but Shaw didn't die at the forts base but made it into Wagner before he was killed. When his father, back in Massachusetts heard he was buried with his men, he told the Confederate commander, his body should remain where he fell.

review_headline: I wish I could give it zero
review_body: Only ordered it on Fire TV because it had such a high rating. I give it -5 stars for the "plot" two stupid for words. Acting wasn't half-bad, though. Maybe two stars--or maybe even three, for sheer ability to make a non-plot on life-support almost come to life. Effects were dumb, too. But the moral of the story was good. A+ for that. An average of 1/2 a star then. Maybe. Let's see: Caveman runs through the desert, no water, no shade, no attempt to conserve energy. Caveman who grew up alone meets tribe who moved into the area, and they understand each other perfectly. Caveman kills dinosaur with hand ax. Right. Caveman sees bow and arrow for first time, and shoots it perfectly. Caveman runs to back of cave, fleeing bad guys. Does he get cornered? Heck no. He finds a dam. Dislodge a rock and whee! Away go the bad guys. Right. Caveman finds twin sister, with key to their mystery encased in ice. What do they do? They leave! Why is there ice? Who knows?  Caveman finds a communicator device, and unknowingly turns it on. Naturally, the whole village is destroyed by laser fire, from afar. Connection? Your guess is good as. Caveman sees sailboat for first time, and sails it perfectly. And THEN the plot gets nuts. Absurd, actually. Caveman finds super high-tech evil villain who can appear and disappear at will. Caveman finds computer keyboard, and operates it perfectly. Caveman finds rifle for first time, and shoots it perfectly. The only good thing in the movie was the hot bod on the cave *woman*. Everything else was pretty much as stupid as it could get. Creationists and UFO nuts will love it. But anyone who isn't totally inured to logic should find something else to watch.

review_headline: The magical tale of a greedy record company, a hopeful boy, and his scarf.
review_body:
I’ll admit it- I live under a rock and didn’t really know who Jared Leto was. It wasn’t until I saw Requiem For a Dream listed as one of his credits that I realized I -had- seen him in something before, but aside from that, I had no knowledge of the guy. 30 Seconds to Mars is a band I hadn’t heard any songs from either! But not too long ago, someone mentioned Artifact being an amazing documentary about the band and their struggles with getting out of their contract with EMI. I knew the music business was a shady one, especially when I saw Behind the Music: TLC, where Left Eye went over how record sales work, and just how little the artists get paid when all’s said and done. While we live in a different age of music now, where anyone can put out anything, those who still want to make it big should really watch Artifact before they go signing any deals.

Artifact covers 30 Seconds to Mars’ attempt to get out of their contract with EMI, one of the biggest labels there is. EMI claimed that the band owed them a lot of money, and when they tried to back out of the deal, they were hit with a (wait for it) 30 million dollar lawsuit. This documentary covers everything from beginning to end of that lawsuit, as well as the band’s journey into trying to make a new album while all these issues are going on. You get a good breakdown of how the industry works, what exactly all gets taken out of the money musicians make, how they can end up owing hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars without making a dime from the album, and how stupid the whole thing is. If you needed proof that there are still outdated models of things out there that people still go by and refuse to change, this is all you need to see.

I won’t go so far as to say that this documentary is “amazing” like so many others claim. A lot of what’s here has been out in the open for a long time, and with how it’s filmed, you’re mostly getting half-making of the album, half-lawsuit problems. Like I said earlier, I hadn’t heard any of the band’s music until I watched this, and if I were a fan, I’d probably like the documentary more. As it is, I thought they could have covered the lawsuit more than they did. It’s clear that the stress of everything was preventing them from having as much creativity as they normally would, and Jared Leto seems oblivious to everything that pops up. I don’t have anything against the guy, but he sure didn’t come off as very likable here, even when meeting fans. I’m sure they kept that footage in for fun, but it didn’t look like Jared wanted to be there most of the time. I also wasn’t a fan of the scarf that seemed like he was forced to wear 90% of the time, even indoors, but hey, that’s just me.

The documentary is well-done though, with 30 Seconds to Mars’ legal friends stepping in and really taking it to EMI’s representatives. While the band signed a deal stating that they would put out x albums and do x shows or whatever, there’s a law stating that no one can be under contract for over 7 years. I didn’t know about that law, and seeing EMI try to bully the band into staying with them was really something. There even comes a point where they tell Leto that they’ll contact him “tomorrow” about a resolution, but weeks go by before he hears anything more from them. This documentary isn’t one-sided for the band, rather, EMI makes themselves look bad consistently.

Artifact isn’t bad. I would’ve liked more interaction with the other band members to get a better look at how everyone was feeling about the lawsuit, rather than just Jared. It was nice that they included brief interviews from other artists and people in the industry to talk about how messed up everything is, from Serj Tankian from System of a Down, and Chester Bennington from Linkin Park. 30 Seconds to Mars fans will love this no matter what, and non-fans can still learn some interesting things.

review_headline: Jeffrey Tambour is outstanding, but the rest of the characters make me dislike watching this show
review_body:
I struggled a bit with how to rate this show. I'll speak to my opinion of the entire first season.

To begin with, I'm a serious theatre lover, and someone who hates musicals. I like foreign films and edgy comedy. I really like artsy, boundary-pushing shows. On the other hand, while there was a lot of very interesting stuff in Transparent, and Jeffrey Tambour gives an amazing performance, I didn't really enjoy watching this show. I don't find it funny very often. Mostly, I find it incredibly sad.

I'm not troubled by the level of graphic sex in this show because of what it is, but I did feel while I was watching that I was watching *gratuitously* graphic sex. Much like levels of gore (*ahem* Quentin Tarantino) that seem like a lazy layer of icing on what could be a genius cake, it seemed to me that the characters in this show were so self-absorbed, so pathetic, so unlikeable, that the graphic sex acts as a yellow highlighter of selfishness smeared all over each fornicating character. Maybe, being so old-fashioned as to find sex a beautiful, natural act of love and joy, I'm just not hip enough to "get it" in this series?

I also hold a very liberal position on adults making adult choices, alone or together. The part of this show that I did like was the fascinating process of Jeffrey Tambour's character finally blossoming into the woman he's always known was inside himself. This is sensitively done, and feels very honest, real, and, finally making the title ring true!--"Transparent!"

Is it meant to be a metaphor that the father's years of hiding her true self from the world led to such insufferable consequences in the characters of her three children? This is the part I struggle with. The adult children are all vile. I can't enjoy any scene where they are the center of attention. No amount of interesting story line makes up for the pain I experience contemplating the existence of people like this.

I wonder if this is why Middle America hates the coasts? I grew up in the Pacific NW, and I live in a liberal New England city, but I believe in morality (mostly as what one must live for oneself, not as a threat to hold up to the throat of others.) The very idea that these characters could seem believable to anyone leaves me reeling. I find them very hard to imagine as real.

Toward the end of the season, there's an episode in which the youngest daughter has a bizarre, dis-associative date with a very butch lesbian. That storyline was one of the few I felt was actually pretty compelling and it has stuck in my mind for weeks. More character development like this, that seems like real, flawed human behavior instead of a sociopathic impulse to work as counter to human goodness as possible, could bring me back to give season two a chance.

There is really good acting here, and an aggressively edgy script. I wish the totality of the subject matter made it worth watching for me. review_headline: Very insightful documentary! A must see!
review_body: As a seamstress myself, I hope people see the consequences of the fast fashion industry and consumerism as a whole.  Garment making is no easy task. It takes years of practice and skill to be able to create clothes with speed and accuracy, so with that said, industry workers should be paid what they deserve so that they can support their family, have a roof over their heads, and to have food on the table. We also need to think about what we are doing to our planet and how our natural resources are not limitless. This documentary will help to open up your eyes as to why we cannot keep exploiting our fellow human beings and resources, and just remember, once you know something, you can never unknow it. The next time you go shopping, ask yourself, do you really need new shirt? You are voting with every dollar you spend. Buy local, organic, and fair trade whenever you can!

review_headline: A Must-See...what life trauma do you have to face?
review_body: I live with someone who daily suffers from chronic pain.  What's interesting is that he had a very traumatic childhood...physical abuse from his father.  He experienced broken bones, etc.  Interestingly enough, the movie seems to draw a correlation, not only between a traumatic event and the physical aftermath, but that of the psychological aftermath as well...being just as chronically debilitating.  I find that to be true.  It made me feel compassion towards Anistons' character.  Her mental / emotional trauma transformed into chronic pain, making her life miserable.  Wonderfully acted, brilliantly written and something for anyone to walk away with.  Thank you for such a deeply moving movie.  This is a must-see for anyone wanting to understand what may be an underlying cause of chronic pain...haunting memories, losses and the need to face them all.

product_title: The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo: Extended Edition (English Subtitled)
review_headline: Very powerful and emotional movie, it will get you thinking thats for sure!
review_body:
I just finished watching the Girl with the Dragon Tattoo. It must have been the extended edition because the movie seemed to run very long. I was hooked very quickly by the story and watched all 3 hours which goes by very quickly. This movie is very graphic especially the scenes with Lisbeth's guardian or caseworker. It should definitely be for adults only or those mature enough to handle the subject manner. Even then this film might turn some people off.

The movie itself is a murder mystery suspense film. It is one of the best films in this genre that I have seen in quite some time. This is the kind of movie that keeps you glued to the TV where you don't want to be distracted or take any breaks. The suspense is riveting and the film will keep you on your toes the whole time. There is no point in summarizing the movie several reviewers have already done that. Just rest assured that the movie is definitely worth watching and is far superior to the Americanized version with Daniel Craig and Rooney Mara.

I did not mind the subtitles at all. A couple of times I had to rewind because they talked a little to fast. But I much prefer a director use the subtitles than over dub the language in English. Where you can tell the actors are not using the right words out of their mouths.

Noomi Repace and Michael Nyqvist really own the roles of Lisbeth Salander and Mikael Blomkist. I thought they did a fantastic job throughout the film. I found the film very authentic and believable for the most part. I guessed the real killer about midway through the film and turned out to be right. But finding out all the twists and turns was well worth the time all the way to the end.

The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo is the rare film that will keep you thinking the whole time you watch it. The characters are flawed people who make mistakes and that's what makes it believable. They don't seem like cookie cutter characters with no flaws or obvious weak links. I found it ironic that such a wealthy family's extensive bookkeeping held the clues that eventually put the puzzle together. I would give this film 5 stars but definitely know what you are getting into before you watch the movie. review_headline: I usually like a decent police drama and therefore liked Bosch
review_body:
I would probably give Bosch 3.5 stars but half stars were not an option. I usually like a decent police drama and therefore liked Bosch. It was fairly gritty with some dark brooding humor. It had some solid performances and told an interesting fairly realistic story. There was a good look at the politics, ass kissing and inner departmental douchebaggery that managers would likely claim does not exist in police departments.

There were some times that the story bogged down a little. Seemed like it got a little long winded and clichéd as it went on to get all the episodes filled. And then there were other times I thought they put on a well above average representation of an investigative process. Then something less than well done or cliche would happen and kind of pull me out of the story.... I'm not sure who takes the blame for that sort of stuff but I assume it 's the director. One such example is when two of the leads are sweeping a residence, and found damning evidence of a crime. The audience has seen the felon go in and out of the garage multiple times and knows clearly where the garage is and what the doors look like. But when these two seasoned partner detectives get to the doors one announces out loud to his partner and the audience, "garage." I assume this is done because the partner detective could not possibly have ever seen a garage door before? (facetious)

Apparently, the military that captured the chiefs were not too competent in keeping them in captivity, as several escaped regularly. It seemed that the writers could have done a better job with at least two hours, or better yet a series for each individual chief.

review_headline: Hoffman is Brillant in a Complex and Dark Film
review_body: Philip Seymour Hoffman was exceptional as the German Case Officer attempting to penetrate and monitor the Muslim community in Hamburg for possible terrorist cells as part of a special unit in German Intelligence that operated on the edge, and often beyond it, of constitutional legality to build his networks. Rumpled, a chain smoker, overweight, he is  the antithesis of popular notions of intelligence operatives who are frequently portrayed as handsome, supremely confident with extraordinary physical endurance and strength.  Despite his everyman appearance he is a shrewd judge of character, as case officers who run sources must be, and possesses a moral code that is revealed as the movie proceeds and for me was the most interesting facet of his persona.  The film takes a deliberate approach to the subject allowing its principle characters to be revealed as much more than the usual Hollywood caricatures this genre of film habitually trots out giving time for the viewer to better appreciate their motivations and the difficult circumstances they find themselves in. Phillip Seymour Hoffman's hard edged empathy is frequently on display.  Hamburg serves as an excellent setting for the story to evolve as Hoffman and his team attempt to achieve their result while others in the German Government and the CIA are watching and waiting.  Not only an exceptional film but a reminder of what film lovers lost in  Mr. Hoffman's tragic death. Please see it.

review_headline: They Never See You Coming Do They Bob?  A Classic Movie Line That Fits Perfectly.
review_body:
Before seeing this movie I read the screenplay which is based on Dennis Lehane's short story "Animal Rescue". As is common in the movie business, the book is far grander in scope and plotting. HOWEVER--and I don't get to say this very often--THE DROP is an intelligent movie adaptation that more than compensates for the subplots eliminated from the book. It is smart, it is witty, and it presents a hard working neighborhood in Boston in an appropriately gritty way. The characters are well described and are fleshed out more than enough to justify their status in the story. Actor Tom Hardy takes the part of Bob Saginowski and turns it into what should have been an Oscar nomination. It's well worth watching the movie just to see the finesse with which Tom Hardy portrays a character who shows no affectations (emotions of any type) moves in a slow and ponderous way, runs a bar efficiently, does the necessary dance with Chechen criminals, and yet handles the major challenges he faces with coolness and confidence.

The story uses an abused puppy, found torn and bleeding in a trash can at the beginning of the movie, as a metaphor for the life of Bob Saginowski. Bob has spent most of his life in a very limited geographical area, like the puppy in his cage. He has been subjected to the school of hard knocks, has been maligned and misjudged, and yet is always able to interpret what he sees around him and solve whatever problems come his way. The other thing about Bob is that everyone seems to love him. The supporting cast does a great job of reinforcing Bob's character and his importance in the movie, just as a supporting cast is supposed to do. Almost at the very end of the movie, the detective who is investigating all of the criminal action in the story, leans close to Bob's ear and delivers a line that not only perfectly summed up the movie, but also kept me laughing out loud for five minutes. Watch the movie and wait for the line. It is truly great stuff!great stuff!
much better than i thought it would be

I’m someone who will never understand the hype of “viral videos” and the celebrity that comes from them. It took me awhile to figure out why people were drawn to watching outtakes of Jack Rebney swearing. It all became apparent who Jack really is about 20-30 minutes into the film.

I like Jack. I think there is a whole side of him that the director failed to capture. It was as if the director wanted to mold him into some version he had in his head before driving out to meet him. He missed out on capturing the real Rebney when he asked him to “tone down the political stuff.” (Ever think that’s where the anger stems from?) And the shots outside of Wal-Mart and Best Buy? Why not shoot them from the car after being told to leave the property? I would’ve loved to hear what he had to say.

I think Rebney would be an excellent political/social commentator. I feel like I can relate to him (and his anger)—being frustrated because Americans seem content being ignorant while corrupt politicians run amok and ruin the country… Too bad a different director couldn’t have made this movie. There’s probably an even bigger fan base (other than from YouTube) that would’ve liked to see Rebney explain his hatred for Dick Cheney. And share more of his (oh dear…here’s that word) POLITICAL views. Anyways, 5 stars for Jack Rebney, one star for the director.

review_headline: Story is full of cliches and shallow characters
review_body:
While I do love Ryan Reynolds and think his performance was pretty solid, the movie plot and writing was rather meh. The movie starts of nonlinearly, which only serves to confuse rather than as a useful storytelling device. After we finally get onto the "real" timeline, there are then unexplained time skips between scenes where you are only able to know what time you're in because the characters keep saying "6 years since she disappeared" "8 years since she disappeared" etc. If you're going to make it that blatant, just put a scrawl at the bottom of the screen that says "2 years later". All of this basically makes me feel like the producers read about nonlinear storytelling, thought it was a cool idea and did it with no understanding of HOW to use the device correctly.

Aside from that making things a little confusing, the story itself is lackluster. There's no real mystery to it at all, as the only "suspect" the cops ever have is the father himself. Which on many levels is incredibly infuriating beyond the obvious of making the cops look completely incompetant. It's like: a girl is missing and you spend hours interrogating the dad? They don't even *think* he could be telling the truth? And the one "bad" cop guy is suspicious because he thinks no kid would ever lay down in the back of a car? Yeesh. They try to explain this "bad" cop guy's dislike of Reynolds by saying he "knew a guy like him" once that he was investigating, but again the writing falls short because we never find out what "guy" he's talking about or how that case went wrong. Just hollow character building.

And the worst part about the whole movie to me is the mother's hate towards Reynolds. She of course blames him for their daughter missing, despite the fact that it makes no sense. Maybe at first in the heat of the moment, but jeez really lady? And of course it doesn't help that the cops are basically pathetic and can't do their jobs, thus placing blame on the dad as well.

Anyway, the story is lackluster, there's no real mystery to solve since the kidnapper is revealed from the very start and the cops have NO OTHER suspects, ever. And even the kidnapper makes no sense. Obviously he took her because he was a pedophile, but then still keeps her because... she apparently agreed to help lure other kids in? But oh, don't worry, she's still a good person and is not psychologically messed up in any way.

The story is good. The idea isn't too bad but there are some major annoyances. There are some -SPOILERS- in this review.
1- cinematography. everything is in soft focus 100% of the time. I'm not sure why they chose to have everything slightly out of focus. And they needed to invest into a tripod or a better steady cam. Not everything needs to be shot free handed.
2- the screen writers suck really bad. A lot of the time there was drama just to fill up time so it gave it a tacky soap-opera feel. It desperately needed a rewrite. If they had, it could have been very good.
3- A third of the actors were just overly annoying. But that could have just been the bad screen writing. Maybe it's the director's fault. Maybe there wasn't a director.
4- the monsters. really? I mean REALLY? I've never seen anything so weak. has anyone ever thought of using rope? Ear plugs? Maybe just pushing one over? I mean, they just stand there then ever so slowly approach. Then !0 years later they'll scream. And there's no inclination that they possess any abnormal super strength. Soo..... It leaves one to wonder if everyone in Moscow gets their head hit with a baseball bat on a regularly scheduled time, just to reinforce the retardedness. Don't get me wrong, they are all 9-10 star super hot looking models. I felt bad for them whenever one got shot because they were so cute.
5- The 3-5 minute long recaps at the beginning of each episode. Sure we can skip it but do people have that bad of a memory that they need a recap of every part of the story? For all I know they have 1 episode a month. Then it would make sense. It was almost as bad as Heroes 10 minute long recaps.

This is a limp, cynical marketing ploy masquerading as a film. Ferrell and Hart are likable enough (and seem to like each other), but they have zero comedic chemistry, and their pairing here has a lot more to do with corralling "urban" and "frat pack" audiences into the same theatre than with doing anything remotely fresh or creative. Set pieces that aim for inspired zaniness fall completely flat (Ferrell trying to fellate a guy or say the N-word). The normally manic and unhinged Ferrell (on display as recently as the Campaign) is grossly miscast, left with both comedic hands tied behind his back, and Kevin Hart does never crosses over from endearing to funny   Plot-wise, this is the same core premise we've seen in any number of Martin Lawrence, Damon Wayans, or Eddie Murphy films going back 30+ years to "Trading Places": Dorky and/or racist white guy gets hip and learns valuable life lessons via a chance encounter with a fast-talking black guy. Seriously, this film has all the biting socio-cultural satire of "Bringing Down the House." It's like an early 90s comedy aimed at baby boomers got lost in a time capsule and unearthed in 2015.  Finally, the production values are on par with a late-period Adam Sandler film. Visually, the film feels boring and utterly generic. Even Ferrell's bad orange dye job reveals the sloppiness and laziness at work here--this is a total phone-in-for-the-paycheck film and represents a low point in Will Ferrell's canon. If he's going to select such formulaic, paycheck-driven roles, he could at least choose ones that allow him to improvise and play to his comedic strengths.

review_headline: Even if you have watched every other series like this, watch this one
review_body: Thinking this might be derivative of any number of WW women related productions from the BBC lately, I was not expecting too much from this drama.  I guess that means, with such midland expectations, I had an even more pleasant reaction than expected?  It is brutal.  The relationships are complex.  The consequences of one simple act, like showering with a necklace on, can have dire results.  One of the senior staff is played as a sociopath (or something close to it) so, every time one hopes she will really be kind this time, she does something quite the opposite.  This review sounds like the program is tawdry - it isn't.  It is a well played drama with a sad trajectory as it should be when dealing with WWI and the front.  I learned, too, where the "Crimson Field" landed in the pecking order of medical caretakers having no idea they even existed.  From that standpoint alone, it was a satisfying experience.

While this series was engaging and thoughtful, the whole experiment seemed doomed to failure from the beginning.  It seems nearly impossible to take people from the present with current cultural experiences and thought and suddenly dump them into a civilization of a century ago.  The characters cannot forget where they are truly from, and that knowledge colors their daily interactions greatly.  It was no surprise that the only ones who truly enjoyed the experience were those privileged few who were chosen to be aristocrats and at the top.  The major surprise for me was the attitude of the tutor.  I understand his feeling of not belonging to either the aristocrats or the servants, but his behavior was certainly not professional or admirable.  The actions of most of the other characters were predictable.  In all, this was a difficult undertaking and showed the pitfalls of trying to recreate the past.

review_headline: A Clever and Creepy Found Footage Horror Flick That's Sure to Give You Chills!!!
review_body:
Most of the time I'm against, or rather tired of found footage type horror films. Earlier this year, Unfriended came out. I saw it and I truly enjoyed it. When I first saw the teaser trailer for this, I didn't really know what to expect. When the real trailer was released, it looked a lot better. I saw this film yesterday, and I also truly enjoyed it, almost as much as Unfriended. It was short, scary, creepy and to the point. I can't believe it's getting such bad ratings. As long as I feel scared by the atmosphere, the lighting and shadow of the ghost, the jump scares, the tension, and if the ending is good, then I'm happy with it. Just the thought of going to an abandoned dark school at night, being locked in by a supernatural presence, and being stalked and killed is a very scary concept to me.

In 1993, the drama class of Beatrice High School is performing a play called 'The Gallows' Near the end of the play, a boy named Charlie is set to be hung at the gallows. A freak accident happens when the door beneath Charlie's feet opens and he falls through with a noose around his neck, killing him and traumatizing the whole school.

In 2013, a new group of students are finally going to remake the play the way it was meant to be seen as a tribute to Charlie. The man behind the camera is Ryan, going around the school and filming his friends as they rehearse and prepare for the play the next day. Ryan's friend, Reese is set to play the part Charlie had. Reese has a crush on the girl wanting to redo the play named Pfeifer. Ryan soon comes up with an idea to break into the school at night, and destroy the sets so the play can't go on.

They soon realize every school has its spirit when Charlie himself comes back from the dead and begins stalking and killing them all in the dark and deserted school. In conclusion, I really thought this was a decent little horror flick that deserves some more attention. It's miles better than Paranormal Activity. review_headline: The Pacific is well-produced, riveting tale of a confrontation, without glamour, between the Unites States and Japan in WWII.
review_body: "The Pacific," a micro-look at the United States' WWII-in-the-Pacific-theatre experience, is riveting television. The plot lines -- based on real-life characters -- are compelling and illuminating. The series follows the experience of a handful of Marines engaged in some of the most difficult military actions of WWII. The stories are personal and detailed. One episode, which tells the story of the US involvement fighting the Japanese in New Britain, portrays an even more challenging encounter -- a war with tropical weather. Weeks of drenching rain drive the men to distraction, taking a devastating physical and emotional toll on them. Overall, this series is well written, well acted and beautifully produced. And the final episodes -- on the battle for Okinawa -- portray the tremendous heroism demonstrated by Japanese and American soldiers, locked in a struggle to the death. They also clearly demonstrate the cost of what might have happened if the United States had not used the atomic bomb to blow the Japan's leaders to their senses.

review_headline: M. Night Shyamalan produces another masterpiece
review_body:
I first watched The Village two years ago when I was twelve and loved it. I hadn't heard anything whatsoever about it before then, so I didn't have any expectations regarding the storyline. Contrary to what I believe most people expect prior to watching this film, The Village is not at all a horror film. It certainly isn't as scary as The Sixth Sense (which was Shyamalan's best work in my opinion), and in fact, isn't intensely scary. Aside from one prolonged very suspenseful scene about half an hour in, the movie moves slowly--but not in a bad way at all. I think the reason this film was frowned upon by critics was because they were expecting something this movie certainly is not. This is a drama about an isolated village in the middle of the woods, not a suspenseful horror movie.

The Covington Wood surrounds a settlement in 1897, as depicted by a tombstone in the beginning of the film. Everything seems idyllic: There is no need for any currency; everyone is neighborly, and, aside from the fact that the film opens during the funeral of a seven-year-old boy, everyone seems happy and content. But the viewer soon discovers everything is not perfect. For in the woods lurk Those We Do Not Speak Of-- viewed as both horrible creatures and guardian protectors by the villagers. The elders of the village have established what they call a "truce": we do not go into their woods, and they do not come into our village. The 'bad' color, red, must never be visible, for it attracts them. And heed the warning bell, for they are coming.

The movie brilliantly portrays the theme of oppression through fear and delivers an unexpected twist in the last five minutes. This is one of my favorite movies, and I hope this review changes the opinion of a would-be hater.

review_headline: Entertaining little dramedy with very appealing cast and scenery.
review_body: I bought this on DVD when it first came out in Britain and thoroughly enjoyed it. The cast was comprised of very talented and funny artists and the Scottish scenery was surprisingly sunny and oozing warmth. The children were delightful, rather than obnoxious, as the entertainment industry is wont to portray them.  Their dialogue was semi-improvised, with a key line being fed to the kids and then the adults were left to react as the children riff on the theme. The results were very funny and endearing. The kids and Billy Connolly absolutely owned the show, relegating the divine David Tennant and lovely Rosamund Pike to supporting roles. The darker themes were handled with aplomb by the children and adults alike. The final act dragged a bit with a few too many threads and was anticlimactic after a mid-show twist, the characters were not as fully fleshed out as I would have liked them to be. This is the reason for only four stars.

I like to watch dance movies and enjoy watching Patrick Swayze dance so, after reading other people's reviews on this movie, I thought I would watch it. The opening dance scene was very good. However, while I enjoyed the dancing in the movie, I did not enjoy the movie itself. The dialog and plot seemed disjointed and underdeveloped. The acting lacked depth. The three main characters are in their 40s, are passionate about dance, and come together to dance again. Each of them had ended their dance careers prematurely for a variety of reasons. So they grapple with ghosts of their past and bodies that are past their prime to pull together a dance. At the end, the dancers deliver a dance that seems to close the doors on the past and push them toward a brighter future. One dancer gains confidence and the other two renew their commitment to each other. In summary, the movie started well and ended well. The material in the middle was mostly forgettable.

review_headline: Pseudoscientific nonsense: for the faint of reasoning and uncritical of thinking.

I was blissfully unaware of this hodgepodge of pseudo-scientific nonsense until recently. I watched it tonight, and found it full of tortuous pretenses of rationality, and based almost entirely on flawed understanding of scientific knowledge and scientific methodology.

Watch for: magical thinking, abuses of quantum theory, category errors, tossed word salads, incoherent platitudes, contrived teleology, and deep dives into shallow thoughts.

If you have any grounding in reality or strive for objective truth, you'll alternately laugh at the nonsense and cry at the misrepresentations of science. If you're rationally lacking and blindly credulous, you'll love it.

Trigger warning for rational people: Hitler water (Masaru Emoto)

product_title: The Celts - The Complete First Season
review_body: Highly informative. Covers the entire known history of Celtic peoples in Europe, from Neolithic to Modern times. Places special focus on interaction with the Roman Empire (an entire episode, while the dark ages and Medieval Period get only one episode for both). Watching this, you get a real sense of who these people were, how astonishingly large their influence was (all the way from Gaul to isolated settlements in China), and how greatly they have declined since, being pushed westward to the British Isles and Ireland. Woefully, the entire series spends a brief 30 seconds on the Manx and their relationship to other Celtic groups; it focuses largely on Scotland and, to a lesser extent, Ireland, from the Industrial Revolution on. Nevertheless, an interesting series, worth watching if you're wanting to really learn about the Celts and not about what people THINK the Celts were or are.

review_headline: The best of the best and a fresh new take on Terminator awesomeness!
review_body:
I have been endlessly fascinated and captivated by the Terminator story line ever since I saw the first one as a kid back in '84. Naturally T2 blew me away like it did most everyone else at the time of it's release, and through the years both have proven to be permanent staples of what my imagination craves. I never tire of anything Terminator related and still watch the first two movies multiple times every year.
I didn't hate T3. It was, in my opinion, a good effort at advancing the Terminator mythology, but it somehow failed to deliver in certain ways that left more to be desired. Terminator Salvation had my hopes high for an all out post Judgement Day setting where surely Skynet and it's merciless army of machines would clash with John Connor and his resistance fighters for the ultimate spectacle of Terminator awesomeness. Man was I thoroughly disappointed in the shortcomings of that dud.
And don't even get me started on how much my heart broke when the Sarah Connor Chronicles got axed by a short-sighted network. Some wounds never mend...
So needless to say I was both excited and apprehensive when I first caught wind of a new Terminator movie in the works, especially when the word trilogy was thrown around. I always want more Terminator, but quality over quantity is what matters to me. I went into the theater earlier this week for Genisys with high hopes, but low expectations.
After 5 viewings to date, I can honestly say it's the Terminator movie I have been wanting since the credits rolled for T2. I was riveted by the whole thing from start to finish. The post Judgement Day future sequences were phenomenal. Exactly how I've always imagined it would be. In fact, the movie hit virtually on every point and theme which makes the Terminator universe so awesome and enthralling.
The 1984 segments gave me chills. The movie definitely recaptured some of the magic and coolness from the first two films there while adding something fresh and exciting at the same time. Then the time-hopping to 2017 really set the stage for the twisty, action-packed second half. Even knowing about the John Connor twist beforehand didn't take away from watching it all unfold and impacting the plot as the race against the countdown to Skynet's arrival began. And the confrontations which ensued between opposing forces were nothing short of breathtaking and thrilling. Having two different Terminator models which can go toe-to-toe in brutally bashing battles certainly amped up all the exhilarating action sequences too. wink emoticon
The story was very cleverly contrived also, revealing bits of intrigue as it progressed while leaving some very interesting questions to be asked. It's the kind of story like the first two, that both satisfies and leaves you wanting more. The nods and ties to existing Terminator mythology was great too. This movie felt like a complete Terminator story, thanks in large part to the events of T1 and T2 which were crafted in and built upon to reach new territory in the franchise.
It was really fun to see familiar characters again too, even if the faces were new. Mostly anyway. Arnold was just as awesome as always as the venerable T-800 that really is the staple of the Terminator universe if you ask me. The way his age was accounted for was just brilliant storytelling that worked. Emilia Clarke's Sarah was feisty and strong willed with a nice touch of humanity to keep her from being a cold, bitter victim of fate. Jai Courtney's Reese was loyal, dutiful, and filled with enough bravado to make him the time traveling soldier/protector he was destined to be. I enjoyed the conflicting chemistry between Kyle and Sarah that developed thanks to the changes in events which changed expectations, but not the feelings they would both ultimately succumb to for each other. Jason Clarke's John Connor oozed delectable charisma in both his incarnations. He was an intriguing and formidable villain just as much as hewas a heroic and revered leader of men. And the addition of J.K. Simmons' O'Brien was a welcome injection of a new believer in the Terminator saga.
One more thing really worth mentioning too is the musical score of Genisys. The modified versions of classic Terminator music and sounds were incorporated masterfully into this new story. Thanks to the excellent use and timing of the incredible musical score, the action scenes were pulse-ramping, the poignant scenes had increased depth, and the overall movie had nostalgic vibes which somehow felt fresh and exciting. I really cannot praise the composers enough for the way the music and sounds helped to fuel this movie.
So is Genisys a flawless movie? Of course not, but to me it's about as perfect as a Terminator movie can be. It didn't disappoint on any level to me, and whether or not sequels are built upon the rubble of Cyberdyne left in it's wake, Terminator Genisys is the success I've always hoped for in this franchise.

review_headline: A suspenseful horror film perfect for October
review_body:
* spoilers *

Bobby, Zack, Jeff, Mikey, and Brandy are on a quest to find the most extreme and obscure haunted houses. They are tired of the sugar coated amusement park crap and want something more. Together they embark on five day road trip across the South in their RV to backwater haunted houses with dubious legality. With their winning personalities and disregard for other people, they piss off a few of the haunts in their wake, leading to some tense and dangerous situations. One such haunt seems to be following them wherever they go, no matter how far away. Are they regular people just angry at them? Are they criminals or something more supernatural? The group also stumbles across the most extreme of haunts called Blue Skeleton that needs clandestine meetings and secret passwords. Will it be what they're looking for or will it prove too dangerous?

In the past, I was never a fan of haunted houses and horror mazes because I've always been high strung. In the past few years, I finally went to various theme park Halloween events and had a blast. The characters in the film are tired of these events and want something more. I enjoyed the documentary type segments where they question scare actors, fans of these events, and creators of haunted houses. Their quest begs the question where should the line be drawn? There can only be so much done and guarantee the safety of the guest. The faux documentary explores a little of what people do to make their haunts more extreme: employ actual psychopaths and criminals, allow the guests to be attacked, use of actual body parts, and even the accidental inclusion of actual death. I can see signs of this in the real world, especially in the attraction Blackout where guests sign away their rights and are then manhandled, waterboarded, tied up, and sexually assaulted. I think this film is an answer to this growing trend.

The narrative story of the film is equally interesting to the documentary bits. The style is found footage, which I don't have a problem with when done well. The main source is the group's cameras as they film their trek, but also other people's cameras, security cameras, and the like. I enjoyed the videos through all the different haunts. It starts off fairly standard with mainly jump scares which you can see in any walk through a horror maze., Then it builds suspense in the rest of the film and really creates an atmosphere of dread. The later haunts although not horrible worse lose the air of fun and become more alarming. All is fun and games until the first haunt and then a clown wouldn't move from the front of the car, just staring menacingly. Then the creepy porcelein doll girl followed them over a hundred miles to freak them out with her maniacal laughter and it escalates from there. One of the best scenes of the film is when the whole troupe of scare actors stood in front of their RV in the middle of the night after scaring the friends awake and then suddenly disappeared. The very end with the last haunt is taut with tension and I was on the edge of my seat.

Unfortunately, the film falters in a few places. The characters are fine, but make some dumb decisions and are unlikeable at times. The guys are very bro-like and macho. They cause trouble for no reason at all or maybe just for their own amusement. Brandy seems totally against the entire endeavor and doesn't seem to even enjoy haunts. It begs the question why she's even there except to have a stereotypical screaming, hysterical girl. The very ending is so very disappointing. I get that the filmmakers wanted it to be vague and up to interpretation, but it seemed more like a copout. You never really know if the characters die at the end. I don't think they did, but the ending would be pretty anticlimactic if they were shown to survive. The Blue Skeleton haunt isn't completely unknown, so it is doubtful at best that they could succeed in murdering people every single year.

The Houses October Built is a well constructed film that builds tension and suspense right up until the end. The makeup is impressive, especially when contrasting the very real looking Blue Skeleton scare actors' makeup with all the others that are more typical and slap-dash. Even with my problems with it, I had a great time watching it. The feeling of dread in the pit of my stomach when I watched it is more important than the small details. This is a perfect movie to watch for Halloween and I will put it in my yearly October watch list along with Halloween and Trick 'r Treat.

review_headline: AN EXCITING SET BY THE LEGENDARY DIZZY GILLESPIE AND HIS OCTET AT "CONCERTS BY THE SEA"
review_body:
Five EXCELLENT Stars! This Amazon Instant Video is the 1986 Gary Keys film that captures Grammy-winning Hall of Fame trumpeter and bebop innovator John Birks “Dizzy" Gillespie and an octet of excellent jazz musicians recorded live at Howard Rumsey’s ‘Concerts By The Sea’ in Redondo Beach, Ca. The octet includes the multi-instrumentalist and multiple-Grammy winner Paquito D’Rivera on alto sax, Hall of Fame double bassist Ray Brown, Ed Sherry on guitar, the fleet-fingered Valerie Capers on piano, the renowned composer and arranger Tom MacIntosh on trombone, Michael Howell on electric bass, and Tom Campbell on drums.

The set begins with a sizzling uptempo version of Gillespie’s classic “Bebop” which features fiery solos by altoist D’Rivera, guitarist Sherry, Gillespie, and drummer Campbell. Then they play another Gillespie classic, with the expected Gillespie spoken introduction about the ancient African empire, the mysterious and compelling “Kush”, with great solos by D’Rivera, MacIntosh, Brown, and Gillespie. “Birks Works” is taken at a mellow tempo and gets bluesy, swinging solos from Gillespie, Capers, and Howell, but Ray Brown takes the solo honors with a display of facility and imagination that reminds us of why he is one of the top 5 double bassists in jazz history. The blues number of the set is “Hard of Hearin’ Mama” features Birks both as trumpeter and 'blues shouter' and the double-handed pianistic fireworks of Valerie Capers. The set ends with a funky song with breaks where Gillespie inserts the names of jazz musicians of the past: Hawk (Coleman Hawkins), Miles, Art (Tatum), Pres (Lester Young), Roy (Eldridge or Haynes), and Earl (Fatha Hines or Bud Powell). Directed by Stanley Dorfman. This set captures Dizzy Gillespie and his cohorts at the height of their musical abilities before an appreciative jazz audience in a venue where I have spent a few enjoyable evenings. My Highest Recommendation. Five EBULLIENT Stars (JazzAmerica Ltd & KCET Community Television production. Color. Not Rated. Closed Captioned commentary. review_headline: DEAD CROSSROADS:  It's dead alright.  Dead Boring. *yawn*
review_body: I am always up for a good haunting show, but that's not what this show is all about.  This is the "Cliff Notes" of some anciet ruins, lots of broken windows, rubbish, concrete slabs, gaping stairwells, creaking doors and hinges and....not a darn thing more. We get a dizzinying quick-march step tour of a few buildings which have fallen into spooky depths of despair: but no tales of the legends born within, nothing more than CN intoning "Here, in this room is the kitchen"...Thought the two guys who we rarely clearly see are experts, however watching them crawl around these dilapidated sites without anything more, equipment-wise, than a weak flash and a ball cap.  And............that's it. A tour of nothing but night goggle clarity, all green walks and chambers  of the paths and crooked, tortuous stories in some cases; but nothing more. They say they spend the night but each story only lasts for 15 or so minutes; there is never anything there either, except the narrator's tired and atonal, a droning sound-announcing THIS spot is wherre we will spend the night. Roll credits. The thing is over, never having done much of anything except waste some money.  I watched the first two, got fed up with the noxious narration, and so switched this mess off. Great for fans of deserted and likely disease-ridden ancient bacteria filled historic dumps. Maybe the Clampetts could feel at home here.  It's no "cement pond", though. Do not waste your time.

product_title: Heaven on Earth: The Rise and Fall of Socialism - HOUR ONE
review_body: Excellent documentary.  I am writing this after watching both parts 1 and 2.  The documentary gives both an insightful analysis of the philosophy of socialism as well as an engaging narrative of how it played out in various regions around the world (USSR, UK, Israel, Tanzania, etc.)  Philosophically, the attraction to socialism is that it provides a basic humane standard of living - guaranteed for all people regardless of their life circumstances.  This philosophy is extremely powerful in places where the poor live extremely harsh lives and the rich are very powerful and living in high opulence.  The problem has always been the inefficiency built into the system: if those who work hard don't receive much more of a reward than those who don't work at all, then their incentives to be productive is severely diminished.  If the government runs an industry, it does not have nearly the same incentive to control costs and to make sure that the services it is providing are valued has highly as the resources it consumes in order to provide them.  Also, elements of abuses of human rights and authoritarianism are discussed in certain socialists systems (e.g. China under Mao).  Well worth watching.

I caught this movie while channel hopping. I am not a big Jack Lemmon fan and had never heard of Judy Holliday. But the young Jack Lemmon filming people in a park was strangely funny. I stopped long enough to see the early true talent of Jack Lemmon and see Judy Holiday for the first time. What an absolute treat. I believe that many actors do their best work when they are so fresh to making movies and or stage. We are able to see actors work so hard to perform and often see what has caught the eye(s) of someone who recognized their unique, wonderful talent. Both Lemmon and Holliday have a unique style and works together delightfully well in this movie. Also, the young and handsome Peter Lawford was perfect for his role and a joy to watch. At age 59 I have more of an appreciation for the work of actors in their early years and find it a real treat to have caught this movie by accident. The treat was the joy the movie gave me, as I cracked up at Gladys Glover and all of her verbal and physical responses to situations and questions. I researched Judy Holliday only to see that her life was cut short by breast cancer. But for those minutes that passed as I watched the movie, Gladys Glover is not unlike any of us that take a dream and turn it in to a reality. Something that our spirit has sparked or created in us, and we own it. While others tell us we're crazy, we move stubbornly on, somehow knowing it's a great idea and no one will deter us. And if you stay focused and on track "It Should Happen to You."

I have to say I was very disappointed in this Season! The first Season owned so much more of a historically accurate feel. Whereas this Season feels like a soap opra where everyone wears long skirts. Elizabeth made her mind up in the end of the first season to stay in Coal Valley and that she cared enough about Jack not to leave him behind. Somehow in this season she questions herself all over again?

Elizabeth is much more judgmental and critical of everyone else, while she herself is leading two men on without considering their feelings!! It contrasts so much with her character in the first season, when she would have given advice freely but wouldn't have been pushy about it. She treats Jack really poorly, and doesn't open up with him until the last episode...

Jack, however, was much more like his old self, but how could he be completely that, when he is still pursuing Elizabeth, who is so different from what she used to be and the girl he first met??? You really end up feeling bad for him and kind of wishing he would just move on?? In real life...most guys would.

The hair/dress styles were shocking at first! Their hair was a little over the top modern, which would be beautiful for me to have, but somebody in the early 20th century??? In the country?? I appreciate when people make an effort to show faithfulness to history, and this show just shouldn't be set in 1911 anymore. The dresses were so modern, like something any girl could find at a JC Penny's! In the first season, every dress looked so authentic...

Oh! And Abigail is still sweet, but I think they should drop the idea of a relationship for her and Bill. Although he might not be "bad," it seems like a waste of time to keep their relationship open, when he wasn't honest with her? I think she should marry the pastor...it seems like he has a past, but at least he's humble/honest about it with her!
So disappointed in how they changed the show! Therearen't anymore well-thought out mysteries or in depth stories...you only see a little of EVERYTHING! Also Miss the character Cat Montgomery, and other characters who portrayed faith in God, perseverance, and simplicity.

I appreciated some of the stories and was disappointed that they didn't go into them more! :(
Rosemary becomes one of your favorite characters, and Julie seems like she is way more loyal (and even wise?) than Elizabeth! Rosemary and Lee have the best relationship in the show...they're very straightforward with each other. And at least Julie and Tom want to get married...and they aren't playing around as much as their older siblings!

The first 5 or 6 episodes aren't worth watching...choppily done scenes, etc. Adding the character of Clara didn't make sense! She wasn't a good actress, didn't fit in well with the story, and ended up disappearing in the best episodes anyway?

In the end, I hope that if they make a new season, they'll take some advice from the audience. Otherwise, I hope this will be the end so the series doesn't go even further south! The main reason that I put four stars on the season instead of three, was because the last episode was a little more reminiscent of the first season. Elizabeth was finally more honest and kind with Jack, although she should have apologized. :/

After seeing this season, I believe my favorite "When Calls the Heart" is the original movie. It spoke a message about clinging to Jesus Christ no matter what difficulties come our way and the parents loved their daughter enough to encourage her. I miss seeing Elizabeth's sweet relationship with her dad! In this season, her dad was so snobbish and almost creepy. :/

review_body:
Oh man, what can I say? This was beautifully done, the acting was perfect, and I could not stop thinking about it, it really got to me...
I 'thought' I read that it was a romantic comedy, but it is anything but that, well, it is, and it isn't, I don't think I have seen anything like this before, it definitely surprised me, and that is a good thing. Steve Carell is a really good comedic actor, but he's equally as good when it comes to showing what he can do in a dramatic part as well. He can flip back and forth between the two, in one scene, that is not an easy task for most, but he does it flawlessly. This guy can act!
As far as Keira Knightley goes, to be honest, I am not sure if I have seen her in anything that I have watched, if so, she did not make an impression on me. THIS movie however, she did really well, I started out not caring too much for her part, but by the end, I really appreciated her acting skills.
My wife and I both loved this, we didn't have great expectations, but it affected us both, me maybe a little more, I guess because I was more in the mood for something like this, I don't know really, all I know is it punched me in the heart.
The bad part is, I really love Steve's comedies, his style, so, now, the cat's out of the bag, everyone will want him to do more serious roles, so maybe his movies won't be comedy related, at least, as much. I know that he has done other dramatic movies, and I have seen some of those, but they were not in the same class as this was, in my opinion.

review_headline: Small Budget Creates A Very Big, Important Movie
review_body:
I was born in the closing weeks of WW II so there was zero chance I could do my part although my parents did theirs. But all my life I have felt a certain guilt that I was not able to do something to contribute to that epic battle to literally save the world for Democracy.

The men and women who lived through, and fought that noble fight and those that never made it "home" deserve our ever lasting gratitude and eternal respect.

They were, and will always remain, for me and for so any others: "The Greatest Generation"

I try to watch every film, that like FORTRESS, makes us pause and think how I would have withstood the non stop horror, the constant fear, the continuous awareness , 24/7, that maybe today or tomorrow or next week, my luck will run out and I also will just become another statistic, returning home in a Flag Draped coffin.

In the very opening of the film one reads a brief text that the men we are about to "meet" in this film belonged to Divisions where you had to complete a minimum of 25 successful bombing missions before you could be relieved from further future flying missions. And this statement was followed with the words that only 2 out of every 25 flying groups ever survived long enough to complete their required 25 bombing runs to be relieved from those Divisions.

Those are pretty thin odds. And how many of those brave flyers did make it home but without arms, legs, faces and/or their eyesight to gaze once more on those they loved and had left behind.

Those who give a film like this less than 4 or 5 Stars, because the film had a limited budget that did not allow for all the Hollywood glitz and special effects one encounters in a 10 or 20 Million dollar Mega production miss the whole point of the film.

And likely such "film critics" were not there, did not serve, do not have the faintest clue as to what it was like to be there at that time in history.

I grew up around such people who were there, in those planes, who were among those who were part of the waves of soldiers who stormed the beaches of Normandy, literally forced to run into the onslaught of German machine gun fire as soon as they stepped on the beach.

How many of those brave men were simply cut down the moment their boots touched the sand, cut down in the prime of their life.

Some may say that the negative critics here are simply rating the film according to their personal expectations of what a film must contain and achieve to be considered a 5 Star film.

Well, good for them for being so demanding and so "discriminating". And how admirable that they have the boundless "courage" to turn off and stop watching a film that does not cut it for them and/or make the grade according to their lofty expectations.

I wonder just how courageous such demanding critics would have been if asked to board one of the bombers we see in this film and fly every single day into the Jaws of Hell.

For me personally I want a movie to envelope me with its story and its message and make me think and feel and be moved and remember all the characters and their faces and their dreams and yes- their ultimate Sacrifices freely made for the sake of Humanity.

I do not need to watch a 40 million dollar "Star Wars" type spectacle to feel I did not waste my money or two precious hours of my life, which I can never replace.

When I view a film I hope it will make me think about life, about what others have done and sacrificed, before me, to make this a better world for those who follow.

And FORTRESS achieves that in Spades.

And for the record, those who gave this powerful movie just 1 or 2 Stars- that's probably 1 or 2 Stars more than such people would have ever received in the Military- if such people had ever served in the Military in the first place to protect the Nation in which they lived.

Bravo and bravo encore to the Director, the Writer, the Producers, the Actors and all who took part in bringing FORTRESS to fruition. It is a Film which will endure for generations to come.ESS to fruition. It is a Film which will endure for generations to come.

product_title: Rolling Stones - 1969-1974: The Mick Taylor Years
review_body: Interesting, fun and informative.  Produced on a shoestring budget, but who cares.  The Stones were operating at a peak during the Mick Taylor years (and "Beggars Banquet"), and produced a series of the finest rock/blues/country records ever, ending with "Exile".  Has any modern pop band put four such masterpieces together, one after the other (maybe Duke Ellington or Frank Sinatra?)?  Then Keith became a junkie and Mick resigned himself to a worse fate: hanging around with the glamorous and glitterati, and it was a descent into parody except for the occasional bomb, e.g., "Start Me Up".  I remember the first time I placed the needle onto "Rocks Off".  That opening Keith riff, the snapping snare, Mick's "oh yeah".....  Fantastic, just so incredibly good.  This documentary describes all that and is worth a look for the more serious Rolling Stones fan.

product_title: Small is Beautiful: A Tiny House Documentary
review_headline: This film is about the people building a tiny house, not about actually building or living in one.
review_body:
It would be more accurate to say this is a documentary about 4 people who decided to build a tiny house not about how to build one or what its like living in one. So from the start my expectations were disappointed. There were several discussions about designing the house and the issues each ran into while building, but nothing in real detail. I was expecting to see a start to finish showcase. Maybe showing where you can get plans, how one might alter them ( and what tools would be needed to do so ), where one should look to find a place to build it, builders resources, what to look out for and avoid, and maybe a what I would have done differently section.

What I got was a documentary spending as much time with the reasons each person decided to build a tiny house and while they did show each home it different stages of construction, there were no real details for how it was done. I will say the documentary was well done if you were looking for back story for why people might choose to live this way but not at all helpful if you wanted to know what it was like to build and live in one. I also have to say this is not a feel good documentary. Each person (or couple) featured in the film have dark pasts and unresolved issues driving them to make these choices. I was genuinely touched by their stories and hope all of them find their way to peace. But if I'd known it was a film focusing on people not on the process of building or changes required to live this way I would not have purchased it. I'm giving it 3 stars as it was well done but not at all about “what its like to build and live in a tiny house”.

review_headline: Best Sci Fi in a Generation
review_body: This is the best SciFi film in a generation. It's Godzilla meets Blade Runner with a little Fantastic Voyage thrown in. First and foremost, the story is a creative and original take on the old Japaneses monster movies, Godzilla in particular. But this film goes so far beyond that, it's simply a paean to those earlier works and not in any way a copy. Pacific Rim is an original story with plenty of plot twists and surprises. The acting may not be top notch, but neither is it a hindrance. The sets and cinemaphotography are excellent. Special effects are good but not the best. That having been noted though, the story line is so strong that the film does not rest on effects alone. The story moves itself along. If you are not a SciFi fan (as I am), expect a 6. If you are a SciFan fan, I call it an 8-9. Very, very good film.

You may, or may not remember the Saturday mornings watching the kitschy 70's Batman with Adam West and Robin in their sorry fitting tights, bad dialogue as they scaled sky-scrappers, hand over fist, making jokes and throwing punches with big POW's over head? Plz! This is what comic book fans of Batman had to endure before Tim Burton's Gothic film of a stylish crime-fighter as he transitions from Batman to Dark Knight without the process. This to me is the best to date comic book adaption of Batman/ Dark Knight out: darker with sinister undertones in an unrecognizable metro, murderous villains, cool gadgets, car and the best bat plane, and directed with Tim Burton's flairs for stylized emotion, goth and humor. The staccato tempo of the music fit the heroes antics and the bizarre atmosphere of a city gone bad. Fine performances from Nicholson, Basinger and, of course, Michael Keaton, but not as Bruce Wayne so much. There are moments by Nicholson of brilliance in his mad Jokers theatrics that were Oscar caliber. Writing, directing, and the sets were original and superior to anything before. Vicki Vale's mannerisms played well off of M. Keaton's brooding hero and his facial expressions fit the mask and expressed what the writers, or Adam West, couldn't get from the character, the quiet determination and strength of a possibly mentally ill anti-hero. This is the classic.

I'll keep using this video because my kids like it but I prefer Preschool Prep for more focused learning.

product_title: A Journey to the Highlands (Original UK Version)
review_body:
I started on Downton Abbey on Amazon Prime because of its high ratings. Season 1 was slightly boring but enough for me to stick with it. The characters were nice, and there were lots of them. The plot ran smoothly. There was just one character I disliked greatly from the first moment: Mr. Bates, and Anna's love for him was offensive to me. He's old, he fat, he's crippled, and he's an idiot. At one point even he said, "I'm a stupid, stupid man!" What can a beautiful young girl like Anna see in him??? Eventually almost all the servants liked him and I never saw why: he couldn't do his job as valet because he's crippled, so they had to pick up the slack. He wasn't particularly nice or helpful to anybody. What's there to like? The even showed a scene of Bates and Anna in bed. Fat old guy with beautiful young chick. I was traumatized by the sight!

But the rest of the characters are very nice and colorful, each with their own unique personalities, strengths and weaknesses, and the storyline flows right along -- until the last episode of Season 3. I watched some of it and then quit before the end, so I never saw the car wreck (that I read about later). I just felt like a story has gone past its end. It's like this thing is never going to quit. I'm bored. The show has fallen from being a great story to a soap opera. It's like the author ran out of ideas and doesn't know when to quit. And my patience has run out.

review_headline: Took some time but Enterprise has grown on me.
review_body:
I'm a big fan of TNG and Voyager. Stuck with both series until the end and still watch them over and over. I watch DS9 occasionally. When Enterprise first came out on broadcast television, I watched a few episodes, but didn't find them to have the "feel" of the other Star Trek series. I didn't find Scott Bakula's interpretation of a Captain to be along the lines of the other Star Trek Captains, but that improved. It was very obvious that they chose Jolene Blalock to capitalize on the type of draw the Jeri Ryan brought to Voyager. I thought that was kind of pathetic that they felt the need to do that to bring in viewers.
A few weeks ago, I decided to try giving Enterprise another chance and now that I'm into season 2, I do enjoy it. What I like best is how the crew reacts when they encounter new aliens. In the previous Star Trek shows, they all acted like it was no big deal. In Enterprise, it's still something new, something they're not accustomed to, just yet.
I still don't feel like this series had the same "mojo" as the others. That might be why it never got the fan base and ended after 4 seasons.
I will hope that another Star Trek series will happen in the future, but one that offers the action and intensity that current tv viewers are interested in. A Sci-Fi series needs to be as almost as good as a movie.

You really understand how smothered her life has been and why the life of a street clown is glamorous to her, and the ability to perform without inhibitions to really put herself out there. I think the film is not so much about this subculture of street clowns but more about our journey in life and finding ourselves along the way.
And I like that it isn’t the same old movie using the same old clichés, the addition of the street clown makes it unique.
I highly recommend watching Courting Chaos and checking out Alan Clay’s other movie, Butterfly Crush – and his many books.
