review_headline: It might be a dying art-form, but it's not dead yet
review_body: As much as hand-drawn animation is being supplanted by computer animation, there are still artists who know the power of the art form and give us beautiful images that go along with great stories. Sylvain Chomet (LES TRIPLETTES DE BELLEVILLE) has done just that with THE ILLUSIONIST (aka L'ILLUSIONNISTE, and not to be confused with the 2006 Edward Norton film). The story is rather simple. It is about an out-of-work French magician/illusionist who goes to Scotland and meets this young woman who is convinced that his "magic" is real. Over the course of the film, you see a friendship develop between them as his livelihood becomes less viable as a means of support and she comes into her own as a woman. Aiming for subtlety, there is hardly any dialogue (intelligible dialogue, at least) and the images are the primary driver of the story. It's also quite touching and heartfelt. You really feel for this aging man who sees the life he's built for himself as a magician grow smaller and smaller as people now go to the music halls to see rock bands instead of illusionists, ventriloquists and clowns. By the same token, the woman has to discover that the "magic" isn't what it appears to be and, in a sense, grow up. From a technical standpoint, the animation was just beautiful and a sight to behold. Sylvain Chomet has a very distinctive, impressionistic approach to character design that makes each frame look like it could be a watercolor painting. Also worth mentioning is that the film is based on an unpublished script by Jacques Tati. Although I've yet to see anything by him, the comedic sensibility on display here makes me want to do so really soon. When all is said and done, THE ILLUSIONIST is a mature, wonderfully animated film with plenty of humor and heart that every animation fan should see.

product_title: The Hobbit: The Battle of The Five Armies
review_body: The movie's many strengths come in relatively trivial aspects of the film, while its weaknesses fall in what should have been the heart of the tale. Martin Freeman, alone, saves the film from disaster by providing a believable, deep, affecting characterization of Bilbo. Ian McKellan is again believable as Gandalf, though relegated to the role of a sort of magical Jeeves. Though criticized as written in as "something for the girls," Evangeline Lilly does a good job, too. The rest -- the characters, the storyline -- is all middle-schoolish baggage. The different dwarves (with a couple of exceptions) are basically interchangeable Smurfs. As far as characters, Freeman has to carry the whole movie, and even with astonishingly lame dialogue, he does. Whew! As important as characterization, and as weakly done, is setting. For what is supposed to be a believable, whole new and other world, scene after scene looks like either the painting it is, or a Lego project (which I assume will be on the market). I assume this visible fakery was done deliberately, both to mimic the fake reality of video games and to provide visual continuity with games derived from this movie. But the clunky settings, combined with the godawful Brothers Hildebrandt meet Thomas Kinkade lighting come close to ruining any believability at all. Ditto for most of the CGI. Viewing the elven army is about as interesting as trying to read graph paper. I know those guys are precise, but I haven't seen anything look so mass-produced since those awful Gungan army battle scenes in the Star Wars prequels. The effects nearly sink the film, but, ultimately, there are plenty of enthralling, beautiful, and surprising images that save the day. But wow -- what a hefty load of junk as well. Many of us don't want Jackson to be a strict constructionist with Tolkien, but to do as he has sometimes done and make the works anew, as film. So adding characters, expanding stories and details -- fine. But as has been the case for this whole series, Jackson has lost his way. It's no even close to the story of Bilbo Baggins, or some other kinds of story. It's just a load of stuff strung together by a sequence of events that we don't really care about, happening to people we don't even like (with a few exceptions). It is essentially Super Mario Brothers 3 (the old NES game) in both plot and presentation -- right down to the jumping block-to-block sequences, right, Legolas... again? -- though with somewhat less spirit and far, far less charm. But I suspect that's the idea. Peter Jackson and his mature, adult friends making something for "the kids." But while Tolkien elevated the reader, and worked from a basic concept of what is noble, deep, best (and also worst) about people, Jackson is just selling stuff. There's something for everyone in here. That's why I gave it it 3.  And it's also why it has no possibility whatsoever of being a 5. Few will watch it twice. In two years, no one will watch it at all, let alone talk about it. Or care.

review_headline: The guilty are buried with the past...
review_body: A uniquely dank beach town overrun by greedy mobsters sets the stage for a tale of deception and mayhem as actor/producer Keith Collins lingers this masterpiece back to the old haunting style and wit of Alfred Hitchcock macabre.  Throw in a hint of M. Knight Shyamalan's epic thrillers with a dash of Wes Craven's knack for innovative slasher films like "Scream," and you'll find your attention glued to the screen waiting for the killer's very next move.  "Gravedigger" sets itself apart from lackluster plots and cheesy characters that leave the viewer saying, "you really expect me to believe that?"  Collins is of no disappointment either, giving a stellar performance of the stoic yet enigmatic defense attorney Steve Borden - a man  grappling with a guilty conscience from a prior case that went terribly wrong.  As Borden's personal turmoil transpires, a serial killer known as the "Gravedigger," is stalking and murdering all those he has deemed guilty.  Will burying the guilty burn the gravediggers own guilt? Can Borden bury his own past?  "Gravedigger" sends the viewer on a rollercoaster ride of parallel twists and turns unlike any other movie in the suspense realm.  You won't want to miss this!

I approached this film with much trepidation given the starkly mixed reviews it has received. I seldom agree with the Academy of Motion Pictures about what is worthy to receive the “Best Picture” Oscar, so I braced myself with low expectations.

Wow! What a film! I loved it. After now seeing it twice, I can still say that I love it, maybe even more so.

This is a great film. Never before have I had an answer to that password-reclaiming security question “What is your favorite movie?”. I do now. It’s Birdman.

Other works that I have loved that could have pointed me in the direction of this film were Life is Beautiful, The Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind and Shakespeare in Love. Though I didn’t like Moulin Rouge when I first saw it, its cinematography enticed me to view it a second time, and that experience continues to live with me. I also remember really enjoying the novel One Hundred Years of Solitude by Gabriel Garcia Marquez, though I read it many years ago and remember almost nothing about it. What lingers is the heady, intoxicated feeling induced by the author’s magical realism, and that aspect is an important ingredient in this film. As disparate as these works seem, I believe that you will agree with me that there are points connecting each of these works with this film and if you liked all these others, I suggest you will also like Birdman.

Other reviewers are right when they say this film isn’t an action movie, but they’re also wrong because there isn’t one moment of respite in the entire film. All action is not external. The main character’s struggle against his internal demon is the animating force for this story, and I found it riveting.

Other reviewers are right when they say this film is a comedy, but there is almost nothing funny about it. It is a comedy because it is a drama that ends hopefully, even triumphantly. A man puts everything on the line to achieve a goal and in the end he achieves it -- a demon is quieted, relationships are healed and artistic truth is exalted. It’s redemptive in that all the people associated with him in this crazy endeavor are exalted with him.

The message of this film works on every level. You go to a theatre looking to see an action movie (“Batman, Birdman, what’s the difference?”) and this movie slaps you in the face. Though you might have expected to see some mind-numbing action porn to go along with your popcorn and soda you are rudely awakened by a call to a deeper experience. I believe that it is for the sake of that deeper experience that the director and producer struggled to make this film, but it is also for that sake that the main character of the film struggles. He is the protagonist in a fictional superhero series, but he hates himself for it -- prostituting himself to the masses for celebrity and fame while giving up on what initially motivated him into this profession -- a complimentary note scrawled on a cocktail napkin from a celebrated short story writer who saw something honest in our protagonist when he was just in high school. To right himself in his world, our main character sets out to write, act and direct a play all about the man who scrawled that note -- a man who fully embodies the tragic life of the struggling alcoholic writer (not unlike our main character). But his artistic vision is clouded by so many obstacles, some of which include incessant clamor and seductive appeals from his internal demon inviting him back to the life he knew, but also surprisingly from forces dedicated to the altar of high art on which he is preparing to sacrifice himself -- prejudiced against him because of his earlier success in the shallow movie industry. As a member of the audience of this film, we move between the play within the movie, the movie itself, and the larger theme this movie addresses -- each one asking what it takes to be relevant. It’s heady, intoxicating stuff.

Perhaps the greatest conceit of this film -- and perhaps the underlying reason for some objection by some reviewers -- is the tight link made between artistic growth and personal growth. The redemption of our main character as an artist parallels, and maybe even fosters, his growth as a person. I want that to be true, but I know of true-life examples in which artistic growth and personal growth don’t seem intimately connected. The actors in this film give performances worthy of every possible accolade and award, but one of the most astounding feats is their capacity to act badly when the script calls for it, as it does occasionally when our main character is playing his part in the play that he has written. He gets better at it -- and at life -- as the play and film progress.

There is no superfluous character in this story. Each one comes to this endeavor with his or her own very personal angle and perceived vulnerability. It takes almost no time for the director to establish the essential themes for each and every character. They wear multiple hats, though no one more so than the main character who is at once the tormented soul, beleaguered actor, stressed producer, novice director, scorned father, disappointing ex-husband, distracted lover, newly expectant father and former superhero series star. Special mention must be made of the outstanding contribution by Ed Norton. He is a lightening rod -- a galvanizing force singularly dedicated to what is real, in all circumstances and extended to a fault. His character mentors Michael Keaton’s character. He is willing to teach him the ropes because he sees in him an authentic struggle to pursue artistic truth. Just as the internal play comes alive when Michael Shiner (Ed Norton’s character) enters it, so too does the film come alive.

Juxtaposed against “the real” is the fantasied life of the superhero series star. The magical realism in this film helps us understand the gravity of the decision the main character must make -- to choose to keep or relinquish the fantasied power and its associated fame and fortune, even if keeping it feels like selling out. No doubt a similar question lives in the mind of the director. The end of the movie conveys that he can keep his power even after his redemption, but only after exchanging his black mask for a temporary white one. That may be cryptic for those who haven’t seen the film, but I believe you’ll understand it after you see it.

Highly, highly recommended.dy, intoxicating stuff.

review_headline: The Complete Opposite of what I was Expecting
review_body:
Watching this film brought back a lot of reminders of the 2003 film The Dreamers, and no surprise, that's because they were by the same director Bernardo Burtolucci. Burtolucci reminds me a lot of that other infamous Italian Pier Paulo Pasolini, who often used sex in his films to personify power-relations and politics. But where the two diverge is at the cross-roads of eroticism. I couldn't imagine getting aroused to something like Salo (yikes) but Last Tango in Paris, even at it's most downtrodden, never seems to lose it's sense of erotic decadence, and that to me is what makes this film so interesting.

The film follows Paul, an expatriate sort of character who is like a Hemingway character on a Joseph Conrad binge, striking up a relationship with the beautiful eyed and bourgeois Jeanne. Both find themselves creating a cloistered mad little reality as they spend a few days rendez-vousing in a down-trodden apartment with some bizarre characters. Like The Conformist the film is beautifully lit with carefully chosen pinks and somber blues. Pauline Kael said famously that the film's colors resemble rotting flesh, and The soundtrack is equally good with a main theme overflowing with passion and sex. I wouldn't be surprised if this film was the inspiration for every porn film that followed it.

Though the film is certainly not porn, or even erotica for that matter, because Last Tango aims more to provoke our conceptions of sex rather than tantalize them . As a modern viewer I found the film tame compared to more modern films like Irreversible, though the butter scene was still quite shocking, and yet the film remains enthralling, and at times oddly magical. There is more here than just infamy, there is a profound character study and soul behind what Kael called the film's "primitive force."

product_title: Unseen Tears: The Native American Boarding School Experience in Western New York
review_headline: This is an important but sad film on the forced enrollment of Native American children in boarding schools.
review_body:
These parents were told by "experts" that their kids would be better off sent away to school. Who...would want to deprive their child of what was best?

All these kids were trained to be maids, gardeners, and cannon fodder. There was really no attempt to find gifts in these kids and nurture that.
Is it any surprise that most ended up disheartened alcoholics?

It did not help matters any that christianity was shoved down the throats of indian children. The bible says that the earth was covered in water at the beginning of creation about 6000 years ago and again about 4700 years ago in Noah's flood. Native American have ancestors that were in the Americas before the Bearing Straight closed. An earth under water when the bible says would have killed the Native American Ancestors. If the bible is true, indian children cant possibly exist. Native kids are told these creation stories and have to try to shove down the bit where they ...are nonexistant. The native American plants that became new world crops such as squash, corn, beans, tomato, and cacao (chocolate) also would have been destroyed when the earth was under water. . Native Americans that really understand the dates in the bible and their own native history cant really become christian. These schools get these children to reject their own culture. It essentially leaves these kids with no culture.

These kids were turned from children with families and a culture into orphans with no culture.

You see these people on the edge of Pow Wows. They are in effect watching some one elses culture in the same way they would watch Spanish Dancers or French Ballet. Its now impossible for these people to be indian, but they cant really be white either.

The film depicts a bit of how and why this happened and how the former boarding school students feel about it today.

Imagine if you were snatched from your family at 4 or 5. Imagine that your name, hairstyle, and clothing are taken away. Imagine you are a number...and not a beloved child of some family. Imagine no one sees any gifts or possibilities in you. No one cares if your sad, or lonely.

Imagine if you tried to visit home as a teenager, you realize you dont know anyone there. They all related to you as a baby before and revealed nothing personal. They are all strangers now. Could you really get to know these strangers if ...you are no longer capable of speaking their language?

Imagine you then entered the military for some place to go. You would have no strong belief system or family ties to help process the experiences of war.

Imagine the military gets done with you. What now?

If ....the government wished to psychologically damage these people...this...would be a path to create this damage.

This film emphasizes the boarding school portion of this path. Its worth seeing so the same mistakes are not repeated.

product_title: Wonders of God's Creations: Animal Kingdom
review_body:
This film is excellent. I saw another one from this series (Thundering Earth and Roaring Waters) and it wasn't good at all. But "Wonders of God's Creation: Animal Kingdom" is very well researched and produced ... and is still interesting after 4 or 5 viewings.

The premise of this film is that God must have created the world ... and all the animals in it ... for they are too wonderful to have been created by accident (the only other alternative). And it (this film) goes on to prove this point with examples ... and these examples are convincing. Wow.

My favorite three (examples) are 1) the pacific salmon (truly amazing) 2) the bees (hard to believe) and 3) the monarch butterflies.

Interesting from beginning to end ... with outstanding camera work ... "wonders of God's Creation: Animal Kingdom" takes a scientific approach to the study of God's creations ... and leads us to the hard-to-deny conclusion that God is the creator of all life. Truly a wonderful film.

review_headline: A must-watch for hardcore Adam Carolla fans that falls a bit short of expectations.
review_body:
Having been a longtime fan of Adam Carolla (going back to when he was on Loveline) I've usually been happy with the quality of his work. Adam has a very sharp wit, is knowledgeable across a variety of disciplines and frequently has me laughing out loud when I listen to his podcast. Adam and his podcast team have been promoting this movie for a while so I was excited to check it out when it became available here on Amazon.

Maybe it was all the hype that had me expecting great things, but this film really fell short of what I was expecting in just about every category. Carolla stars as comedian Bruce Miller, who is struggling to make ends meet and whose only fame comes from appearing on a long-dead TV show called "The Bro Show" (a clear reference to Carolla's real life show "The Man Show"). He now squeaks out a living as road comic, spending most of his time traveling and performing in small clubs across the country. The film shows Miller dealing with all the annoyances of travel that will be familiar fare for listeners to his podcast (overhead bins on airplanes, people traveling with "service animals" and not being able to get into his room when he finally arrives at the hotel). It seems clear he wants nothing more than to get off the road and get another TV deal in Los Angeles so he can make some real money and resurrect his career. As added pressure, Miller is a divorced father whose daughter just got accepted to USC and he is expected to pay for her tuition. His agent (played by comedian Larry Miller) doesn't seem to be working too hard to get him any work and the few opportunities that are available leave a lot to be desired.

This film wasn't exactly bad, but seemed to suffer from mediocre performances throughout, with Carolla's being the most underwhelming. For starters, I never fully bought that his character was fed up with the road more than he enjoyed complaining about it. All of the pain that is supposed to be serving as motivation for him wanting a change really boil down to a handful of traveling pet peeves or minor complaints about money. It's one thing to listen to Carolla rant about these things on his podcast but played out on screen they come across as mildly humorous but innocuous moments that anyone who travels for a living is used to dealing with. Carolla says a lot with his mouth but doesn't show much through his expressions and demeanor. Most of the time, he just seems slightly annoyed. Very few scenes reveal any painful truths about his character and the choices he's made that have led up to this point in his life. We get no sense of loneliness or any deep-seated resentment for his more-successful contemporaries that make him a sympathetic figure. Additionally, he doesn't have to make any difficult choices and appears to have a soft landing spot regardless of where he ends up. Even staying on the road for a while longer doesn't seem that bad, especially when convenient solutions to his "problems" are already presented and discussed early on.

Excluding a few bright spots from the supporting cast, this film was a bit of a disappointment. While it still has plenty to offer hardcore fans of Carolla's, it isn't something I can recommend to an average comedy fan and includes too many scenes that don't go anywhere and too many cast members that are underutilized.

review_headline: Nowhere near 5 stars, and here's why
review_body:
Is it godawful? Not exactly... but neither is it worth anything over 2 1/2 stars, which makes me wonder if the distributors had family and friends log into Amazon and play with the ratings. The "most helpful" one here screams "plant". Anyway, the premise is actually pretty good: decent, hard-working guy decides to "settle" for a stereotypical spoiled, pouty girl flight attendant, then days after proposing (in the most unfunny and awkward fashion possible) sees a beautiful woman that captures something inside him. You'd think that despite being predictable, the movie would continue in that direction with pitfalls along the way but in the end he ends up with this "true love" type girl - nope. He falls for her kids (great step 1), but everything else goes in the complete opposite direction - there's absolutely zero romance between the two (sorry, taking her clothes on and off doesn't count as "romance"), his best buddy has no qualms whatsoever sleeping with her, SHE has no qualms whatsoever about sleeping with his best buddy, and meanwhile the stewardess fiancee spends the entire movie pouting to the point of making you just want to slap her. After all that, he inexplicably goes back to his fiancee, chalks up the entire "love at first sight" thing to "c'est la vie!" and you're lefting wondering wtf just happened.

Acting was ok in some parts (main guy was decent) and not so good in others. It's *sort of* worth watching once I guess if you've got absolutely nothing else to do for awhile, but unfortunately it's a big letdown on what could have been a good romantic comedy.

Love these mysteries--complex and byzantine, with maximum plot and minimum gore.  Lewis and Hathaway are well played by Kevin Whately and Laurence Fox...a crime-fighting odd couple whose individual styles--one everyman, one intellectual--play well against each other. Oxford is the unacknowledged co-star of this engaging series.  Its windy streets, cozy pubs, golden university buildings, lush gardens and pastoral landscapes lend ambiance and a warm feel to these well-constructed stories of death and personal destruction.  It is also wonderful to see two women--Rebecca Hand and Clare Holman--play strong supporting roles to the erstwhile crime fighters.  One of the reasons for the popularity of this series is undoubtedly that the four main characters are people you would like to spend time with.  They are smart, streetwise and warm--with just enough humor to lighten a homicide detective's sometimes depressing load, and they clearly care about each other.  I know they stopped making these for a year while Whately and Fox took time for other projects, but I hope they continue.  Lewis' cases definitely make a significant dent in Oxford's population growth, but they are a great way to spend an evening.

An enduring, offbeat, and very human epic. Neatly folded into this little story about a local bike race are powerful themes of class mobility, the decline of American industry, the struggle to construct or escape identity amidst family legacies and assumed ethnicities, and the intricate workings of locality, camaraderie, and nemesis in realizing one's true self. One might expect such fraught and weighty themes in a film by Bergman or Renoir (or lately, Linklater) yet Breaking Away glides through with graceful humor, pitch-perfect character sketches, and a lightness that belies its potency as a portrait of desperation, defiance, and endurance in small-town America. Ultimately, without stooping to maudlin romanticism or contrived Hollywood endings, the film leaves one with an genuine and concrete sense of joy in the durability of the human spirit. An unquestionable classic.

I came across this movie while going through the Amazon Prime choices and decided to give it a try. I'm glad I did.

Be With me is a S. Korean ghost film that's broken into three stories. The connection is through a fortune teller, who has a session with three separate girls. He tells them their lives will change. After that, the film shows what happens to them next.

The first tale was the scariest and involved three female students going into an old school to recover items for a bossy senior. The ghost in this story was definitely the creepiest and the atmosphere was by far the spookiest. It was my favorite of the three stories overall, although the third one was also good.

The second tale is about two friends who run into a problem on campus, when they, and one other student have to compete for a recommendation to a University, which I'm assuming is Seoul University. The ghost story wasn't as spooky as the first. It kind of reminded me of other Korean Ghosts films I've seen in the past. But it's still a decent tale in it's own right.

The third tale was the most light-hearted in general. It involved a male student who has the ability to see ghosts. The story doesn't turn out to be what you think it will be. So if you're expecting a Sixth Sense type scenario, you're wrong. This was more of a Fantasy/Horror tale, with a slight love story thrown in. It was very clever.

In the end I gave the compilation a 4. The stories were all good in their own right, although my favorites would have to be the first and third story. I also appreciated how the tales took time to develop the plots. Each was about 30 minutes long. That was enough time to give a little background on the characters, before the hauntings began.

If you like Korean Ghost films, this is definitely a good one to catch. It doesn't focus on the horror aspect as much as the relationship factor. But the tales were still better than most of the tired ghost films coming out of Hollywood these days. Be With Me is an appropriate title, even if it doesn't help give a hint into the haunting aspect of the movie. There are ghosts. Not all of them are scary, but that's part of the film's charm.Me is an appropriate title, even if it doesn't help give a hint into the haunting aspect of the movie. There are ghosts. Red Dawn (2012) is a decidedly inferior remake of the 1984 Cold War classic of the same name. Of this films many faults, the worst that it fails to give the antagonists any personality. The original film did an excellent job of giving the invaders believable, and complex human personalities; they were fearsome, and at the same time fearful. The enemy commander (in that case a Cuban) was conflicted about his mission, yet cunning and ruthless. The personalities of the enemy played well off those of the American insurgents/freedom fighters, who were also fearless, fearful, cunning, ruthless and conflicted. The result is an interesting, and action pacted film which held the audience's interest.   In the remake the enemy is given only a superficial personality; that of a communist aggressor. We know they're communists because they fly a red star flag, and post large signs in public saying things like "Corporate Corruption" and " You are the victims of capitalism." And we know they're aggressors because...well... they invade the US. But that's about the extent of their identities. They are slow witted, predictable, and more than a little inept targets whose only real function is to be out-witted, and shot down by the American insurgent/freedom fighters. The result is just another predictable, and boring action movie. Ho-hum.  Would I watch Red Dawn (2012) again? Nope  Instead I'd watch Red Dawn (1984)

review_headline: Hmm... how to describe this one... Not terrible, cool DVD art. But, they tried to pack in too much into too small a space.
review_body:
Well, this was an interesting film, but not in a good way... Ultimately, it's an "escaped mental patients in the asylum" flick, like numerous others (including 2011's quite good "Asylum Blackout"), but it falls far short of what I'd hoped for from the trailer.

I was surprised by two things: the stilted acting, and the cliched, boring dialogue (also, unless you are familiar with heavy British accents, you may find some conversations difficult to follow) - unfortunately, those two, combined, made for a very boring, hard-to-endure film. The sets, lighting, and photography, and even the DVD artwork, on a positive note, were quite good, which made understanding the vast gulf between between how bad the acting was and how good the setup was, difficult to understand. In fact, I wanted to like this film so much, that I actually watched it twice, back-to-back, but ultimately it only reinforced what I'd experienced during the first go-round.

What I realized at about the one hour mark was the film, in the end, is just too chaotic and disjointed, and in parts, quite silly as it seemed the filmmakers wanted to cram in every "lunatic asylum" horror cliche they could pack into an hour and 22 minutes. It also contained too many subplots, as a result - too many stories going on at once, instead of a cohesive final product.

Now, where I think they could have succeeded would have been to break this into a three-tale movie, perhaps told in retrospect from a survivor, or a documentarian. But whatever the angle, I think telling this film's story in three distinct short stories could have made for a much better final product.

In the end, I didn't "hate" this film nor can I fairly say it's "terrible" - hence two stars instead of one, but I'd definitely wait for this one to come out on Amazon Prime or Netflix.

review_headline: Not bad at all. Recommended for Bosch fans and for those of police procedurals.
review_body:
A well-done adaptation of Connelly's eighth Harry Bosch novel, "City of Bones." Like pretty much all theatrical adaptations, it's not completely true to the source material. (At least one character dies in the novel who doesn't meet the same fate in this series.)

On the plus side of the equation, however, is the casting of Titus Welliver as Harry. Also add in the writers, who have done a good job of capturing on-screen what Connelly has placed into print. I do wish Amazon had started with earlier novels, however, so that we could actually follow Bosch's character arc to see how he got to where he is at this point in his life.

All in all, though, a very good watch, worthy of a weekend binge session.

product_title: Johnny Weir: To Russia With Love
review_headline: This excellent film has been nominated as "Outstanding Documentary" in the ...
review_body: This excellent film has been nominated as "Outstanding Documentary" in the 26th annual GLAAD Media Awards. While two-time Olympian and acclaimed NBC commentator Johnny Weir lends the film his star presence, it is not focused on Weir: the project actually highlights the Russian "gay propaganda" laws within the context of the Sochi Olympics. It follows the stories of LGBT athletes hoping to compete in Sochi, and offers multiple viewpoints regarding the laws, including the perspectives of Russians themselves. It also features Vlad, a young gay Russian teen in Sochi, and how those involved with the documentary helped him to make a better life. Weir was subjected to heaps of scorn from the US LGBT community for choosing to go to Sochi, and yet he not only made a profound statement during his time there by simply being himself, he also took a huge risk as executive producer and interviewer in filming secretly in Sochi. Beautiful videography, well-paced storylines and very thought-provoking material make this documentary a must-see. Highly recommended!

Hawking is portrayed by Eddie Redmayne, an actor who's deserved his chance to shine for a long time now. His performance is nothing short of beauty, especially considering the movie was filmed out of sequence. His ability to show the many stages of Hawking's illness is remarkably impressive. Felicity Jones' performance as Hawking's wife Jane is equally impressive as we watch her struggle to maintain her husband's condition.

Unfortunately, the rest of the film is not so adept. The film plays out like the very mathematical equations in which its subject envelopes himself. It almost feels like a TV movie in its formulaic sympathy. That's not to say it isn't a tragic story, but its telling did little for me.

For the first two-thirds or so, the film doesn't seem to know what it wants to be: A touching story of a seemingly doomed affair, or a bold statement on Hawking's theories. Ultimately it succeeds at neither, amounting to a light, safe, almost entirely forgettable romantic drama. Even the score, which has been winning countless awards this season, I found indistinguishable from any number of films of the same ilk.

review_headline: Umbrellas have never looked so cool.
review_body:
When I first saw the trailer for Kingsman: The Secret Service, it seemed like a bit of an eye-roller. It looked like a forgettable action comedy with stupid one-liners and standardized action built for people who like movies like Real Steel or Agent Cody Banks. I was wrong. More movies need to be like Kingsman: The Secret Service, and there are three reasons why.

Reason number one: It's rated R. This movie could have easily been chopped up and delivered with a PG-13 rating, good for all ages, sans balls (I'm talking about you, Expendables 3). It wasn't. The action here is fantastic, full of glorious head trauma, exit wounds, and broken bones. One scene in particular - set in a church - is one of the coolest scenes you'll see all year.

Reason number two: It's an original property. Yes, I know it's based on a comic book called 'The Secret Service', but it basically just borrows loose plot points from it. I wish more studios would take chances on unknown entities instead of churning out sequels, remakes and superhero flicks. That being said, I bet this gets a sequel...hopefully still helmed by Matthew Vaughn. When someone else takes over something that he made, we get crap like Kick-Ass 2.

Reason number three: It was fun. It took itself just seriously enough that it didn't border on parody, like the last two Pierce Brosnan Bond movies that nearly killed the series (The World is Not Enough and Die Another Day). There were serious, heartfelt moments mixed in with a ton of levity. It paid a ton of homage to classic spy movies while being a blast to watch. Rarely do I leave movies saying to myself, "I need to own that", but this one fit that bill.

The year is young, but I'm pretty confident that when 2015 is over, there will be no bigger cinematic surprise than Kingsman: The Secret Service. It's not perfect - it drags a bit at points and Samuel L. Jackson's lisp is eternally grating, but every actor aside from him is fantastic (including Colin Firth, which I never thought I'd say), the action is amazing, and the gadgets are fun. If you're into action or spy movies, Kingsman is a must see.

My final grade - A-astic (including Colin Firth, which I never thought I'd say), the action is amazing, and the gadgets are fun. If you're into action or spy movies, Kingsman is a must see.

review_headline: I really enjoyed this glimpse into the life of this uncelebrated United ...
review_body:
I really enjoyed this glimpse into the life of this uncelebrated United States founding father, played by Paul Giamatti. The series exposes a revolutionary who is bound by duty and honor to seek justice and to follow his principles, even at the sacrifice of his personal life at times. He often lacked tact to win the favor of alliances, but was a good judge of character–a characteristic he used to fill key roles in the American Revolution. Also, the series places a spotlight on Mr. Adam's most important and trusted advisor, his wife, Abigail, portrayed by Laura Linney. Despite the era, they are equals in their marriage. He may have been the platform to the public, but she was the fortification that enabled him to stand. She is outspoken enough to call him on his crap, and he's humble enough to admit she's right. Thomas Jefferson is another central figure in Adam's life as friend, though their relationship was often strained. Jefferson (Stephen Dillane) is subdued, enigmatic and fairly charming. I looked forward to scenes with Jefferson. He always had a cloak of ambiguity that withheld pieces of who Jefferson was, or what his thoughts would have been behind closed doors. I would love to see a similar mini-series focused on Jefferson's life with scenes cross-referenced from John Adams.

The series is not always historically accurate (http://historynewsnetwork.org/article/56155), which is unfortunate because the truth would have been just as interesting. Paul Giamatti is a great everyman in this role, not to be looked up to nor to be dismissed. His portrayal allows viewers to walk in the shoes of this historic figure at the birth of a nation.

review_headline: Very Well Written, Directed and Acted
review_body: This was a very good series.  Bosch is a detective who tries to do what's right, and whose flawed background is sometimes used against him.  There are 3 story lines that overlap during the course of this series, and a cast of characters which stays constant in their opinions of the man.  There's also an ex-wife who remarried and moved to Hong Kong for 3 years, taking their now 14 year old daughter and causing a little estrangement between Bosch and his daughter.  Based upon a book by Michael Connolly, who was involved in the creation of the series, it's very well done, and the conclusions of the 3 story arcs are good.  Shortly before the answers were revealed, I had guessed part (but not all) of the second and third stories (which were 2 seemingly intertwined mysteries), although my husband had not; the revelation of the facts that led me to these conclusions was gradual and realistic. I hope Amazon makes a second season of this series.

review_headline: The Harry Bosch Series is a MUST watch, or read or listen to for every Crime Drama fan.
review_body: My wife and I have been listening to the whole Bosch series on Audio tape for many years. In fact, we would take unplanned road trips just to drive and listen to the adventures of Harry Bosch. When we saw that it was going to be a made for TV series we were very excited to say the least. Most people compare the books or audio books in our case to the made for TV series and usually the book always wins out. That is the case for this series but it is no fault of the producers and the writers. You can not take all of the details in an 18 hour audio book and squeeze them down into a 30 - 60 minute, time allotted TV Show. So many rich details can not be included, however, the screen writers did an amazing job of making sure all of the important details, lead ins and characters were included. The best way I can describe it is taking a high resolution photo, rich in minute details, full of vivid colors with millions and millions of pixels and compressing it down to a photo that you can send over the internet. The photo is still the same, the subject is still the same and the photo is still beautiful and tells the whole story. There was only one thing that might have made me give it 4 stars instead of the 5 I gave and that was the meshing together of several of the independent Bosch novels into one story line. I thought about giving it 4 stars and then, as I thought more about it, the "mash-up" or intertwining the stories gave the wife and I a whole new experience, almost like reading a new novel. We enjoyed how well the writers were able to seamlessly blend the stories and we enjoyed the few twists that were not in the audio books. It kept us on edge to see what the writers would do next. All in all, the Bosch series, whether on audio tape or in this series, is an intriguing, masterful and well written series that every crime drama enthusiast should read, listen to or watch. product_title: Bill Maher ... But I'm Not Wrong
review_body:
I liked Bill Maher during the W. years, but I haven't seen him in ages. With his recent comments about the sniper guy, I decided to watch the most recent thing I could find...

He's not a good comedian. When he uses curse words, it seems forced and unnatural. His voice gets high pitched and crackles and he comes off as whiny and childish. He prances around stage with such smugness and dismissiveness that he honestly fills me with revulsion. I also don't think that what he says is particularly intelligent or insightful. It seems like his knowledge of the world is very superficial and he comes off as a newspaper reading blowhard who is too lazy or arrogant to read any books that might challenge his worldview. Instead, he picks strawman fights with the dumbest people or dumbest political slogans he can find. To see someone pushing 60 acting like this is pretty unsettling. It's a shame because the world needs iconoclasts, not egotistical, superficially intelligent Liberal jackasses. I gave it three stars because, in spite of myself, I do get a kick out of him bullying the religious and the stupid.

And with regards to the sniper comment he made a month ago-- snipers ARE psychopaths! It's in the job description. They're soldiers in the same way that animal researchers are veterinarians. What happened to you Bill? You're a caricature of yourself.

review_headline: Jane Eyre, or "Beauty and the Beast"?!
review_body:
After years of owning the book, I finally got around to reading it a couple of years ago.
Besides this particular adaptation, I've seen 6 others: '11 movie, '06 mini, '96 movie, '83 mini,'73 mini, and '44 movie.
In 2008 I purchased The Romance Collection: http://www.amazon.com/The-Romance-Collection-Prejudice-Pimpernel/dp/B0012XIGVE/ , and this movie came with the set.
_____

Don't be fooled by its title, this production is far removed from the book (so if you've never read it, and are seeking an authentic adaptation-- look elsewhere)! The only things that the two have in common are the names of its characters, and a few sequence of events! 95% of the dialogue has been rewritten (and butchered), and some events made up!

Rochester is an insufferable, maniacal, beast of a man! With a constant scowl on his face, and a snappish bark of a tone.
How Jane could have felt anything beyond oppression and disdain is beyond me! Jane's character is even altered; she's borderline bratty, somewhat mouthy, and unreservedly opinionated.
Beyond any and all comprehension she actually loves Rochester (despite his blatant mistreatment of her- especially when she's about to leave)!!
..Thankfully it was only 108 minutes long-- anything beyond that would have been torture!
_________

If you're entirely new to this story, please get acquainted with the book before or after viewing! If you're not a fan of reading (or listening to an audio book), and you'd rather watch an adaptation- I recommend looking into the 1973 or 1983 BBC miniseries. While these earlier productions are a bit dated and theatrical/stagey, they are the most faithful to the book. As for the latest mini series, the only real advantage it has compared to the '73 & '83 renditions, is that it has the modern cinematic feel/experience (meaning the acting & sets aren't as stiff and theatrical). In my opinion however, it's the weakest adaptation to date. The dialogue is more modernized, certain events unfaithfully re-written, and the relationship between Rochester & Jane overly romanticized (when compared to the book).
If time is a factor, the movie I recommend is the '11 (although be advised it begins at chapter 28 in the book, and then goes back to Jane's beginning). There are a couple of deleted scenes that add more background to the story, so you may want to check them out.e-written, and the relationship between Rochester & Jane overly romanticized (when compared to the book). If you want a fresh take on possession and found footage, don't write this one off. It's worth it!

review_headline: Aims high at multiple satirical targets and mostly hits the mark
review_body:
After all of the controversy surrounding the Sony hack and the "will-they, won't they" release strategy, was THE INTERVIEW worth all of the fuss? Of course not, it's just a movie. Still, after removing all of the hype, it was still a really good one. It might not hit all of its satirical targets dead-on, but for what it's worth, it did what a comedy is supposed to do and made me laugh. A lot.

The basic plot, which probably everyone and their mother is familiar with by now whether or not they've actually seen it, is that Dave Skylark (James Franco) and Aaron Rapaport (Seth Rogen) have a TV show where they do celebrity interviews/fluff pieces. When they learn that North Korea's leader Kim Jong-Un is a big fan of the show, they secure an interview with him. When the CIA learns about this, they co-opt Dave and Aaron to kill Kim.

First things first, there is a lot more going on in the film than the depiction of the assassination of a current world leader. Early on, when we are introduced to Dave and Aaron, they use that opportunity to take shots at the banality of entertainment news. Not quite original, and they don't really follow through with it later, but it was still good for some laughs. Even before that, the film opens in North Korea during a televised missile launch and a young girl singing death to America and how great North Korea is. This was funny on two levels: First, for the sheer audacity and shock value, and second, because it's frighteningly close to real life. That was probably the best part of the film, but what follows was still extremely entertaining.

After Dave and Aaron finally get to North Korea, things slow down a bit as Dave begins to buddy up with Kim and we get to see that he's human like the rest of us. Aside from the opening sequence, this is probably the greatest insight the film has into the way North Korea works. Not just a brutal dictatorship, but also hereditary, the Kims are revered as gods. However, once the illusion of omnipotence is shattered, the North Korean people would probably react the way they do in the film. Destroy his image and humanize him, and they would probably never follow him again, much less look at him in the way they do now. The third act brings things back to the pace of the first act, but still devolves into a standard action climax. As for the much-talked-about death scene, I didn't think it was too special but the choice of music was pretty fitting.

When all is said and done, Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg have made a film which fits in nicely with the type of stuff they've been making for the last 10 years, but it was a little better because the material was more current and had some immediacy to it. There was probably a little more anatomy-based humor than I would have liked, but more jokes hit than missed. Overall, if you're a fan of Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg's previous work than you'll probably like this. If not, be warned. For me, I laughed my butt off for two hours and had a great time.owever, once the illusion of omnipotence is shattered, the North Korean people would probably react the way they do in the film. review_body: One gets the feeling that Jamin Winans got a laundry list of criticisms from his previous film INK and tried to make a more mass audience friendly picture with THE FRAME.  I loved INK.  For me, that film has a very special personal/spiritual resonance to it, and despite any awkwardness of style, it had such a strong emotional message about redemption that I feel it is one of, if not the best indie fantasy films ever made.  I covered it lovingly on my youtube review channel.  I'd been looking forward to the Frame for the past few years but when I finally sat down to watch it, I was blown away by the superficial level it took with it's storytelling, implying a link between worlds that makes the plight of each central character meaningless by comparison. Breaking the fourth wall for 2 hours without a satisfying punchline. Don't get me wrong, this film is expertly done for a small budget, it's exciting and tense, but there are no arcs for the characters and no resolution to the problem. What I get from the FRAME is that Jamin Winans wants to work in television, and I think the Frame could have easily been cut to be an hour length pilot, or a 20 minute short.  Definitely rent it first.

product_title: Lady Valor: The Kristin Beck Story
review_headline: former Navy SEAL comes out as a transgender woman
review_body:
This is a documentary of Kristen Beck's coming out story as a trans woman. She is the former U.S. Navy SEAL who served 20 years in the military as the man Christopher Beck (born 1966). She gained public attention after her appearance on Anderson Cooper and with her memoir \\"Warrior Princess: A U.S. Navy Seal's Journey to Coming Out Transgender\\" back in 2013. She retired from the Navy back in 2011 and began her transition.

Despite the bans recently lifted on sexual orientation (which benefits gays, lesbians, bisexuals)... bans on gender identity remain in tact. So transgender people are still not allowed to join any branch of the military.

The documentary, overall, was engaging. It's a fascinating story. It's about going to extremes... the depths one is willing to get lost in in order to deny the truth. Despite having a sense of her female self since elementary school, absolutely no one ever suspected that Christopher was anything but the boy he seemed to be. Christopher grew up looking and doing all things expected of a man. He even got married to a beautiful woman and had two boys. He volunteered to be the toughest of the toughest... deployed as a SEAL 13 times and even earned a Bronze Star and Purple Heart. But he didn't like to come home much because he needed to be lost in his illusion. And trying to come out to his wife just didn't work out. His marriage came to an end after 9 years.

His ex-wife, sons... as well as his mother and some of his siblings all refused to take part in this documentary. It was pretty sad seeing all their faces blurred out whenever they came up. The biggest focus of the film is contrasting Kristen's life as a masculine Navy SEAL to her current life as a woman. There is plenty of footage of Christopher's life in the military and the film plays up the contrast of these two lives to a pretty engaging degree.

However, this is NOT a complete story by any means... it is merely her coming out story, which is fairly recent. I read elsewhere that Kristen started her hormone therapy in 2013 in preparation for her sex reassignment surgery... and also that she WASN'T choosing reassignment surgery. So who knows. The film doesn't talk about this aspect of her transition at all or how far she wants to take it (maybe she hasn't made up her mind). It also never mentions her dating history and gives about a minute to her sexual orientation when she's asked if she prefers males or females. She basically refused a label and said she is currently living in a very \\"gray area.\\" It seemed to be a pretty sensitive topic, at least in this documentary.

So I saw some boundaries here... which I can respect. But, if you are choosing to be a public figure/example, I'd of preferred even more candor. But I wouldn't insist on it, of course. I just saw the whole transition as fascinating at every possible level and it is certainly worth a study.

Her life as a woman is just beginning and I think Kristen's story will be a much more different one in 5 or 10 years. I hope she chooses to follow up with a later documentary. Some of her family may even come around. Some people need more time. And her appearance will probably be much more feminine in time as well, if she wants that-- especially if she chooses to explore more options to support that. Though I must say, I really liked a lot of her contrasts. She was completely unapologetic for all her athletic and artillery skills... and while her body is now pretty beat up after life as a SEAL, she was still shown handling artillery as a woman and seemed comfortable in this \\"gray area.\\" Pretty cool. She is still a pretty tough individual and came off as very likable.

product_title: Turned Out: Sexual Assault Behind Bars
review_headline: Fascinating, well narrated, but disappointing in the limited number of interviewees.
review_body: This is a fascinating, if inherently disturbing subject and video. I find the prison subculture (gangs, isolation, extraction teams, and especially the many ways prisoners make do in creating their own meals) and all the myriad dynamics at play to literally be a world unto itself. I don't know how they pulled off scoring Danny T to narrate this, but kudos to the production team on that one. That said, this documentary does have a couple positives - first, it looks at both sides of this issue: the predator, and the prey. The downside, is that it pretty much focuses on one of each. It doesn't do a good job of interviewing a wider number of predators and victims (or, in some cases, willing participants), and in that way it does not provide as full a picture as I'd hoped. So, it's an OK rental, but you will probably end up disappointed, unless you are one of the unfortunate few who has a term in prison pending, and is looking for some inside info and guidance as to how to behave once the gates close behind them.

product_title: Wild: Reese Witherspoon In The Wild (Featurette)
review_body:
With a Golden Globes nomination for this role already under her belt, Reese Witherspoon has been doing things right lately. Many other awards are pending from film festivals, etc., for Ms. Witherspoon, Laura Dern and their director, Canadian Jean-Marc Vallée ("Dallas Buyers Club"). The script by Nick Hornby ("About a Boy") is based on Cheryl Strayed's memoir: "Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail."

Our distraught heroine sets out on a one-woman 1,100 mile trek along the Pacific Crest Trail, through California to Oregon. Her beloved mother has just died and we can see she clearly is overloaded with both camping and emotional baggage. Flashbacks teach us just how wild she has been, AND we learn how she came by that last name. Over the course of the movie she meets people along the way, some generous and kind; others ...not so much. We also see the elements in her life that shaped her and hurt her.

The cast:
* Reese Witherspoon ("The Good Lie") There's very little Cheryl hasn't done and her psychiatrist can't get her to admit she's sorry.
* Laura Dern ("The Fault in Our Stars") Bobbi is determined that her children will not have their lives scarred by their drunken, abusive father. She is incorrigibly upbeat...to her daughter's dismay!
* Keene McRae ("CBGB") Leif refuses to believe his mother might die, as though thinking might make it so.
* Gaby Hoffman ("Veronica Mars") is Cheryl's best friend, Aimee. Hers is the voice of reason as she watches her friend come undone.
* There is a wide assortment of men who appear and disappear, both along the trail and in flashbacks. Suffice it to say, Cheryl is seldom alone for very long....

The first I encountered anything like this was when I watched "The Way," with Martin Sheen. If I watch enough of these movies, eventually I will come to understand these "trails." Evidently they are marked out, with rest stations along the way and guest books for hikers to sign (Cheryl's comments generate interest among other hikers). Packages can be sent ahead from friends and family to intercept the trekker with replacement items, such as new boots (from REI), fuel, and/or money. She also receives letters from her ex, for which she is deeply grateful.

This is R-rated and rightly so! Expect drinking, drug use, sex, nudity and a heavy barrage of "F" bombs. I had to remind myself I was really watching Reese Witherspoon pull off that bloody toenail! And take off all those clothes! And topple over with that enormous back pack!

I was glad I had the option of closed captions, as much of the dialogue consists of interior thoughts as she hikes. Eventually she decides she'd rather be a hammer than a nail and the music on the soundtrack echoes her thoughts.

review_headline: If you like glacially paced, pointless movies with inarticulate characters, this is for you!
review_body: If I could give this less than one star I would.  I can't believe I watched it to the end to see what would happen but nothing really happened. From the first shot to the last this movie is interminable.  It starts off with Guy Pearce sitting in his car for what seems like forever.  It takes a lot of nerve to open with a single shot of a man with a blank glazed expression sitting in the same position in his car for so long that you think the frame has frozen.  I was just about to fast forward when he finally opened the door. Did the collapse of civilization, whatever that was, make everyone dimwitted, incapable of speaking in whole sentences or speaking at all? And what was this collapse that left everyone having cars and guns?  The main character played by Guy Pearce either doesn't speak at all or repeats the same phrases 10 times for no particular reason and never seems to get an answer- is everyone deaf? The second character played by Robert Pattinson can only speak accompanied by unexplained facial tics and weird body movements (this is supposed to clue us in that he's dimwitted). His performance is so contrived that it's impossible to care about him unlike say Lennie in Of Mice and Men who is also "challenged" (this comparison is really the sublime to the ridiculous) We don't care about anyone in this glacially paced disaster. Without a doubt one of the most pointless boring movies I've ever seen.  The only plus I can say is that I watched it on Amazon Prime so I only wasted time but not money

review_headline: Excellent story and acting, but a bit too graphic
review_body:
I enjoy Denzel Washington in most movies, and this was movie no exception. Going into this film, I knew of the Equalizer TV series but had never seen it, so I was approaching this from a fresh perspective. I therefore can't comment on whether or not they added little nods to the series.

I found Denzel's character fascinating, and I love the way he portrayed him. It was just the right mix of compassionate yet tough inscrutability. I found the juxtaposition of his loneliness and his reaching out to help total strangers very moving, and it's enjoyable seeing corrupt, cruel people brought to such satisfying justice.

On the flip side, while I expected this movie to have some violence, I found it gratuitously gory and graphic in places. I think they could have made the same point without being so bloody, almost to the point of B-movie shock death effects.

Still, I'd see it again...the performances and story were that strong.

Poor, set-upon Dessi, trying to hold things together while attempting to cope with a house full of kids, defend Sharon's honor, and be a responsible surrogate father even though all the rules have changed since his day--and even though he's surrounded by smart, strong-willed women. And on the verge of becoming a grandfather himself! \\"A man needs a pint after all that,\\" he sighs. Amen. The film is enormously entertaining, and its humor springs from all the appropriate sources: character, situation and life itself. It's a sweet treat, full of tart-tongued lines, the humor of truth, and a huge helping of heart. review_headline: It's Not The Film, It's You
review_body:
As I dive deeper into this whole Amazon Instant Video thing, it becomes more and more obvious that this is a service for the "masses." By that, I mean it's for anyone, and you will get people on here browsing for and watching things that would never, ever have been on their radar before sites like Netflix and Amazon Instant. This is a good thing, as it gives smaller, less traditional films more exposure. It can also be a challenging thing because, whether we want to admit it not, not every film is tailored for every audience. Some things are specific, require patience, are strange or challenging, etc. Some filmmakers aren't INTERESTED in having EVERYONE like their film. They understand the realities of their audience.

As all the 1 star reviews would indicate, Enemy is just such a film. To me, it's brilliant. But the reviews are awash with simple "it's terrible" or "it's boring and slow" or "it's the worst movie ever" mentalities. Without sounding too condescending or making too general of a statement, may I say that for the most part, Dear One Star Reviewer, this movie was not for you. And just because you CAN leave a review doesn't mean you should. It's certainly hard to discern and self-evaluate, but do your best. And at the very least, temper your impulse to leave a 1 star review, unless you actually have something critical to say about the film, beyond "it sucks and is slow." The film, from a filmmaking and narrative standpoint, is top-notch; the problems mostly lie with the audience, not the film.

So if you're reading this and you're a fan of non-linear narrative, amazing acting, and cinematography that is as gorgeous as any piece of fine art hanging in a museum, you need to watch Enemy. If you are on the fence about it, just know that you'll be watching not a "slow" film, but a slow-burn film, one taut with tension but one very cerebral. If you aren't interested in those things, look somewhere else, for this film is probably not something you will enjoy. And if you do take a chance on it, that's awesome! But if you end up not liking it for reasons that can't be summed up better than "it sucks" or "it's slow", then don't bother leaving a review. Just my two cents on the matter. I hate seeing a film of this caliber having nearly 1,000 1-star reviews. It's not a fair representation of the film.

review_headline: MORE THE ROLE & IMPORTANCE OF THE BEDCHAMBER AS IT EVOLVED WITH THE  MONARCHY  --- NOT AS TAWDRY AS TITLE SUGGESTS
review_body:
3 1/2 STARS FOR AN INTERESTING PERSPECTIVE ON THE EVOLUTION OF THE BEDCHAMBER AND BRITISH MONARCHY

As you might have guessed, the actual focus of this documentary is not as sensational or salacious as the title suggests. It is more of a history of the importance and role of the bedchamber as it evolved along with the British monarchy, beginning with the medieval era. It is a fairly light overview with a run time of only 1 hour and weaves several topics around the central one of the bed chamber itself. I won't give much away because historians will already know it and those who have yet to discover it would rather watch the program. So, I will briefly mention the structure they follow. The program is narrated by the quirky and animated Dr. Lucy Worsley, Chief Curator of Historic Royal Palaces.

A surprising amount of time is spent in actually describing the construction and fabrics used in various beds from medieval times through the state beds of 19th century aristos and wealthy, to the private chambers of Queen Victoria passing in 1901. Along the way, Dr. Worsley visits many bed chambers from castles, palaces, and great houses, all which have played important roles throughout the British Monarchy. We see the role evolve from witnessing consummation, to ceremonial space and access to power, to a statement of wealth and status, to it's decline of importance along with the Monarchy vs. Parliament. Along this thread of the bed chamber role is woven loosely the story of the Monarchy itself, though that focus often wanes in and out. Indeed, almost the first 15 minutes was almost entirely about the construction of the medieval bed and it's trappings. We see later on many lavish materials and many famous beds. Also woven into this story are numerous anecdotes and examples of critical moments altering the British monarchy, in part, through what happened in the bedchamber and how they went about proving it.

Though I chose to describe this program as several threads woven into a central theme, the truth is it can feel a little unfocused at times as they depart from one theme and focus on another. Sometimes its about the monarchy, sometimes it's almost entirely a story about furnishings. For very serious historians, I am not sure how much it will satisfy. For the casual viewer just looking for a little history, architecture and trappings, it's a light hearted tour through generalities and still worth a watch. review_headline: One season would have been enough
review_body:
I would like to address one aspect of discussion which seems to concern some of the reviewers in this section before I get into the review of the program. And that is the "purchase" of Season 1. Some have expressed concern that they have purchased Season 1 and yet the second half of it will not come on air until later this year. This has led some to believe that they will be charged again for a Season they have already purchased.

In fact, this may be the case. It all depends on the studio and how they market the product. If this so called "second half" comes on air and is still referred to as Season 1, then no further charges should follow. However, if the studio (for what ever reason) decides to list the following episodes as Season 2, then they can charge another fee for the new season.
Take for example the show, "The Black List". A favorite of mine and I watched all of Season 1 (some 20 episodes) and when Season 2 came available on Amazon, I had no hesitation in purchasing it. Well about half way through (in November last year) it was suddenly announced that the "finale" would air and The Black List would not return until February this year. Ok, so along came February and The Black List started up again. I was pleased to find that the episodes beginning in February were still referred to as Season 2 and I have been receiving each episode in my library at no additional charge.
So I guess it all comes down to how the program producers market their product. If a person purchases a Season of a program, then they should
rightfully expect to receive all episodes of that season for the price paid. Any additional seasons would attract additional costs.

OK, so now the program itself. And let me be honest. I have not read any books related to this program and if I had I would NOT try to compare this program to something I had read in a book. Book reviews are book reviews. Movie and TV showreviews are just that and the two have no place together in the one review.

I have watched every current episode of this season and while it, at first, piqued my interest, as it progressed, my interest began to wane, slowly at first and in the end very rapidly. While I enjoy (as much as the next person) tales of "wee things that go bump in the night", The settings were very good, the scenery great and most of the acting plausible. I did not enjoy the on-going narrative by Claire. It gave the program almost a "documentary" feel. While the use of the common language (Gaelic) added some realism, the "whispered" explanations to Claire may have given her some understanding of what was going on, but to us viewers it left a lot to be desired as most of the "whispers" were just that and very difficult to make sense of. While sub-titles have their own set of problems, if they add to the viewers understanding of the flow of the conversation, then they are much better than "whispered explanations".
SEX. Yes, what would any "love story" be without a bit of sex tossed in? But sometimes it can become a long drawn out boring addition to a tale and that is what happened with "Outlander".
As for our heroine Claire, she seemed to have a great deal of difficulty keeping her mind on her ultimate goal, i.e. getting back to her own time and her husband. In the end, she came so close, but if that had happened, their would have been little value in continuing the tale. All of which leads me to believe that it was the old producers trick to try and encourage viewers to come back to a "New Season", to find out what happens.
As for me, I wont be back. As I said I began to lose interest early on and by the end all I could foresee was more of the same being served up over and over again. Will Claire ever make it back to her husband (in 1945) or will she end up staying with her husband of earlier times. I don't really much care and as for Claire, she seemed to enjoy both equally well so I guess it shouldn't matter.
To be sure, if this program attracts enough of an audience for advertisers to want to support it, it will continue on in it's endless and senseless repetition of sex and violence but ultimately the ratings will begin to fall and when that happens, it will not matter at what stage of development the story has reached, it will simply be dropped like a hot coal.

Review: 2.5 stars. The 5 and 1 star reviews are off the mark. This movie has some redeeming qualities but is very much a low budget, suspend disbelief (and beat it with a stick) type of film.

Synopsis: In a middle to lower upperclass neighborhood, there is a killer. The first victim is a popular babysitter, the next are housewives and others. The "hook" for the murders is rampant infidelity...

Spoilers / Comments

The various and repeated snafus of real (as opposed to Hollywood) crime scene investigation are worth mentioning...but could not be addressed in this space. I almost want to call this "Housewives of Jersey Shore" due to the Italian - American cliches of the "neighbors". In brief, this is a slasher / whodunnit where the "trigger" of the killer is infidelity -- which is pandemic in this particular neighborhood. The set up of the "patsy" with the contrived "I had to shoot him" is painful but par for the course for the film.

In spite of all of this, the film did hold some interest (or morbid interest about the next plot point) to keep me watching. The doughy cop sidekick actually shines a bit as the voice of reason and quick reflexes at the end. The unshaven yet attractive (cliche) afro-amercan detective (cliche) also does a decent job with the material and yet in true slasher movie fashion loses about 100 points of IQ near the end of the movie...

Overall, 2.5 stars for the bits that shine through and the potential that existed. Worth a watch if you have nothing better do do or can crack a few cold ones before and during the film and have a truly mediocre experience.

review_headline: I have never seen a movie like this that made me have these kind of emotions
review_body: This movie made me think I was watching my life from 12 years ago.  I was not a sniper, but I was in the military overseas.  All of the flash backs are things that really happen.  You do daydream a lot.  The anger is uncontrollable, you go from 0-everything becomes quiet and you can't remember what you have done for 15 minutes you get so mad.  It wrecks families and messes people up to the core.  This movie shows how war really does change people.  It is very hard for me to put into words unless you have been there and know what I am talking about.  This movie \\"gets it\\" and describes what happened to families that were part of these wars from before they started up until now.  It really hit home with me because I remember watching the towers come down in base housing and my wife being at the on base bank and calling me at home.  I remember getting the call from my Sgt..  The movie hits all the little things right on the head to create this massive vivid experience for those of us who really went through it. I have never seen a movie like this that made me have these kind of emotions. Clint Eastwood and his staff did excellent research for this film.  They absolutely got it spot on.  The critics of the film like Moore, Maher, and others have no idea, in my opinion, what the movie is about.  It has nothing to do with making Chris Kyle a hero, though I think he is.  If you were in these wars or were a spouse to someone who was you know exactly what this movie is about.  It is about the struggles with the family. Shows how it changes someone. Explains what PTSD is to people who might not know.  And a lot of other little details that would take to long to write.  This movie followed my life to the letter (with the exception of the sniper part).  I am very upset what happened to Chris.  I know if he were to still be alive it would be hard on his family. It has been horrible for my family, my health, my career, and state of mind.  God Bless Chris Kyle and God Bless Clint Eastwood for putting out a show that helps explain things to everyday folks.

I really really enjoyed this film, I actually watched it twice through in two days and enjoyed it just as much as the first time. What I like so much about this movie is that it does not glamorize war, nor does it paint the characters as overt heroes. What it does do as present war as what it really is, horrific. Without in the same time not going over the top. Its motif and approach is very subtle. I have read several reviews where this movie has been labeled similar to a Horror genre War story. And I am inclined to agree.
This movie is absolutely intense from start to finish, and the acting by all the actors is top notch. Especially the 5 main characters, where all the actors in my opinion should get an Oscar nod for because they all did a wonderful job.
As a synopsis of the story without giving away too much, we are given a small snap shot of 4 tankers we find at the tail end of the war pushing through Germany. There assistant driver and front gunner has just been killed and the replacement they get is a fresh recruit 8 weeks into the army that wasn't even trained as a tanker. We then follow the characters through a number of battles, where the focus of the story is very much on the Newbie, Norman.
Near the end of the film after we have watched Norman be presented with the unnaturalness of the horrors of war, and be dubbed "Machine" as his war name.
I very much feel that this an allusion to that man, by his nature, must force himself to not feel, to turn off his emotions and be a cold machine to kill and commit the atrocities which war requires of them. I feel this is summed up in one line said by Pitt’s characters to Norman. After pointing out an entire city on fire in the distance. He says "Many have died in this war and many more will have to die before it is over."
The movie is very much a study of men doing what they can to hold on to their humanity by having to do something which by its extremity, killing scores of other men, who are trying to do the same in a matter of moments over and over again.
The battle scenes are intense, and the ending battle fits the title of the movie so well, as we see through these men’s actions the absolute "fury" which they must embrace to force themselves to face their fears and continue to fight. As the Webster’s dictionary definition states of the meaning of the word fury, "unrestrained or violent anger, rage, passion, or the like."
Overall, there is so much that could be said, and read into about this film, and I honestly feel that that was the point.
This movie in my opinion is showing us for once a non cynical side of humanity, that rather than showing us that all men are monsters by nature, that we are violent, uncaring killing machines, which we certainly can be, but points out that by our natures, we have to force ourselves in many ways to be that way. That really brotherhood of man can and does happen, but points out that for us to kill one another, so brutally, forces us to have to in a way forsake our humanity, and then in some way still be able to keep it. I think this notion of war is certainly what humanity needs to keep in mind as we move into the future. That even though what these men did in the end of the film was "heroic" per say, what was still done was also horrific, as we watch Norman pulling away from the scene in the end of the film, he is told he is a hero as he is placed in a medic truck. And we can see on his face such a shock of mixed emotions... It really leaves the viewer speechless, at the depth of what can be taken from his situation and what he has done...

It's the little details, like the American flag with the stars replaced by a swastika, and the many Japanese cars on the streets of San Francisco bearing Japanese-style license plates.  Everything you see rings true, with CGI adding concept-appropriate signs and backgrounds, and even a Concorde-like jetliner for German officials.  I rarely watch TV dramas of any sort, but I am already hooked on this one.  I can't wait until the next episode is released.
